uni-bsc-chemistry.title: B.Sc Chemistry — core papers, unit by unit
uni-bsc-chemistry.description: Inorganic, organic and physical chemistry core units of a typical B.Sc Chemistry programme: atomic structure and bonding, organic fundamentals and stereochemistry, thermodynamics and kinetics, electrochemistry and equilibria, and coordination chemistry.

courses.title: Inorganic I · Atomic structure and chemical bonding
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Quantum numbers, orbitals and electron configuration, ionic bonding with lattice energy and Fajans' rules, VSEPR shapes and hybridisation, and molecular orbital theory of diatomics.
outcomes: Learners can write configurations and count radial and angular nodes
Learners can compute lattice energy with a Born–Haber cycle
Learners can predict shapes using VSEPR
Learners can find bond order and magnetism from MO diagrams

scenes.text: Simran writes copper's configuration as [Ar]3d⁹4s² and loses marks. Her teacher writes [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
A completely filled d subshell is extra stable. Exceptions make sense once you know why the rules exist.

steps.title: Quantum numbers and nodes
steps.body:
- n (principal: 1, 2, 3…) — size and energy
- l (azimuthal: 0 to n − 1) — shape: s, p, d, f
- mₗ (−l to +l) — orientation
- mₛ (±½) — spin

Nodes: **radial = n − l − 1**, **angular = l**, total = n − 1.

Filling rules: **Aufbau** (lower n + l first; equal n + l → lower n first), **Pauli** (no two electrons share all four numbers), **Hund** (singly fill degenerate orbitals with parallel spins first).

steps.title: Solved: nodes and configurations
steps.body:
- 3p: radial = 3 − 1 − 1 = **1**, angular = **1**
- 4d: radial = 4 − 2 − 1 = **1**, angular = **2**
- Fe (Z = 26): [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe³⁺: remove 4s first → **[Ar] 3d⁵** (5 unpaired electrons)
- Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-filled/filled d stability)

steps.title: Solved: Slater's rules
steps.body:
Zeff for the 4s electron of K (Z = 19). Groups: (1s²)(2s²2p⁶)(3s²3p⁶)(4s¹).

- Same group (4s): none
- n − 1 shell (8 electrons) × 0.85 = 6.80
- n − 2 and lower (10 electrons) × 1.00 = 10.00
- S = 16.80; Zeff = 19 − 16.8 = **2.2**

This low Zeff explains why K loses its 4s electron so easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming transition-metal ions.
- Mixing radial and angular nodes (a 2p orbital has 0 radial, 1 angular node).
- Writing l = n (l runs only up to n − 1).
- Pairing electrons in a p subshell before each orbital has one.

activity.prompt: Match the orbital to its number of radial nodes.

quiz.q: Number of angular nodes in a 3d orbital:
quiz.why: The number of angular nodes equals l. For a d orbital, l = 2, so there are 2 angular nodes.
Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, not 3d⁴4s². Moving one 4s electron gives a half-filled d subshell, which is extra stable due to exchange energy and symmetry.

quiz.q: Which rule says degenerate orbitals fill singly first?
quiz.why: Hund's rule says degenerate orbitals are filled singly with parallel spins before pairing begins. Pauli limits two electrons per orbital, and Aufbau gives the filling order.
Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s². Losing the two 4s electrons gives Mn²⁺ = 3d⁵, with five d orbitals each holding one unpaired electron.

quiz.q: For n = 3, allowed l values are:
quiz.why: For a given n, l runs from 0 to n − 1. For n = 3, l = 0, 1, 2 (s, p, d).

lessons.title: Ionic solids: lattice energy and Fajans' rules

scenes.text: Kiran heats table salt on a gas burner; it does not melt (NaCl melts near 801 °C).
A Born–Haber cycle reveals the huge lattice energy holding the ions together.

steps.title: Lattice energy
steps.body:
Lattice energy U is the energy change when one mole of an ionic solid forms from gaseous ions (negative, by this convention).

- **Born–Landé**: U ∝ z⁺z⁻/r₀ — higher charges and smaller ions give larger |U|
- **Born–Haber cycle** (Hess's law): ΔH_f = ΔH_sub + IE + ½D + EA + U

Radius-ratio guide (r⁺/r⁻): 0.414–0.732 → octahedral, coordination 6 (NaCl, ≈ 0.52); > 0.732 → cubic, coordination 8 (CsCl, ≈ 0.93); 0.225–0.414 → tetrahedral (ZnS).

steps.title: Solved: Fajans' rules
steps.body:
Covalent character increases with: small, highly charged cation; large, easily polarised anion; cation with pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron) shell.

- LiI more covalent than LiF (I⁻ is larger, more polarisable)
- AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl (Al³⁺ small and highly charged)
- CuCl more covalent than NaCl (18-electron Cu⁺)
- Hence AlCl₃ sublimes and dissolves in organic solvents.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ for dissociating Cl₂ per mole of NaCl.
- Writing EA as positive when energy is released.
- Treating radius-ratio rules as exact — they are guides; many solids deviate.
- Saying polarisation depends only on the cation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl starting from elements.
items: Sublime Na(s) → Na(g)
Ionise Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
Dissociate ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g)
Add electron: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)
Combine gaseous ions into the lattice (U)

quiz.q: Lattice energy magnitude is larger for:
quiz.why: Lattice energy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size. MgO has 2+ and 2− charges and small ions, so it has the largest value.
A radius ratio of 0.414–0.732 corresponds to octahedral holes, i.e. coordination number 6. 0.52 lies in this range.
By Fajans' rules a larger anion is more polarisable, so covalent character increases. I⁻ is the largest, so LiI is the most covalent.

quiz.q: The Born–Haber cycle is an application of:
quiz.why: The Born–Haber cycle applies Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so the formation enthalpy equals the sum of the steps of any route.
In CsCl each ion is surrounded by 8 of the opposite ion at the corners of a cube, so the coordination number is 8 (6 is for NaCl).

scenes.text: Arjun's model kit lets him build a straight H–O–H. His professor bends it to about 104.5°.
Lone pairs push harder than bond pairs, like balloons tied together. That is VSEPR.

steps.title: Steric number decides the geometry
steps.body:
Steric number (SN) = bonded atoms + lone pairs on the central atom. Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.

- SN 2: linear (sp) — BeCl₂, CO₂
- SN 3: trigonal planar (sp²) — BF₃
- SN 4: tetrahedral (sp³) — CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ pyramidal ≈ 107°, H₂O bent ≈ 104.5°
- SN 5: trigonal bipyramidal (sp³d) — PCl₅; SF₄ see-saw; ClF₃ T-shaped; XeF₂ linear (lone pairs go equatorial)
- SN 6: octahedral (sp³d²) — SF₆; BrF₅ square pyramidal; XeF₄ square planar

steps.title: Solved: XeF₄ and ClF₃
steps.body:
- **XeF₄**: Xe has 8 valence electrons; 4 used in bonds, 4 left = 2 lone pairs. SN = 6 → lone pairs opposite → **square planar**.
- **ClF₃**: Cl has 7; 3 bonds, 4 left = 2 lone pairs. SN = 5; both lone pairs equatorial → **T-shaped**, angles slightly under 90°.

steps.title: Solved: ions
steps.body:
- NH₄⁺: SN 4, no lone pair → tetrahedral
- I₃⁻: central I has 3 lone pairs + 2 bonds, SN 5 → **linear**
- NO₂⁺: SN 2 → linear; NO₂⁻: SN 3 (one lone pair) → bent ≈ 115°

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing electron geometry with molecular shape (NH₃ electron geometry tetrahedral, shape pyramidal).
- Putting lone pairs axial in trigonal bipyramids (they go equatorial).
- Forgetting to add/subtract electrons for ionic charge.
- Counting a double bond as two electron domains (it counts once).

activity.prompt: Sort the molecules by shape.

quiz.why: SF₆ has six bond pairs and no lone pairs on S, so steric number 6, which means sp³d² hybridisation and octahedral geometry.
SF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, steric number 5. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, giving a see-saw shape.
Lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, compressing the angle. CH₄ (no lone pairs) 109.5° > NH₃ (one, ~107°) > H₂O (two, ~104.5°).
BrF₅ has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, steric number 6. Octahedral arrangement with one position lone gives a square pyramidal shape.

quiz.q: Lone pairs on Xe in XeF₂:
quiz.why: Xe has 8 valence electrons; 2 are used to bond with the two F atoms, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs.

story.title: Liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet

scenes.text: In a famous demonstration, liquid oxygen poured between magnet poles clings there.
A Lewis structure predicts all electrons paired. MO theory predicts two unpaired electrons — and wins.

steps.title: Building MO diagrams
steps.body:
Atomic orbitals of similar energy and symmetry combine into bonding (lower) and antibonding (higher, *) MOs.

**Bond order = (N_bonding − N_antibonding)/2**. Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond; zero → no stable molecule.

- For O₂, F₂: σ2s < σ*2s < σ2p_z < π2p_x = π2p_y < π*2p < σ*2p_z
- For B₂, C₂, N₂ (s–p mixing): π2p lies **below** σ2p_z

steps.title: Solved: oxygen family
steps.body:
O₂ has 16 electrons; valence MO filling ends π*2p².

- O₂: BO = (10 − 6)/2 = **2**, two unpaired → paramagnetic
- O₂⁺: BO **2.5** (shortest bond)
- O₂⁻ (superoxide): **1.5**; O₂²⁻ (peroxide): **1**, diamagnetic

steps.title: Solved: N₂, B₂ and He₂
steps.body:
- N₂: BO = **3**, diamagnetic, very strong bond (≈ 945 kJ/mol)
- B₂: with s–p mixing the last two electrons occupy degenerate π2p singly → **paramagnetic**, BO = 1
- He₂: (σ1s)²(σ*1s)² → BO = **0**, not stable

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the O₂ ordering for N₂ (s–p mixing changes it for Z ≤ 7).
- Forgetting to count core electrons consistently (count both bonding and antibonding or neither).
- Pairing electrons in degenerate π* orbitals before Hund's rule allows.
- Thinking bond order must be an integer.

activity.prompt: Complete the MO facts.
activity.text: The bond order of N₂ is ___, of O₂ is ___, and O₂ is ___ because of two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals.

quiz.why: O₂⁻ has 17 electrons: 10 in bonding MOs and 7 in antibonding MOs. Bond order = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5.
B₂ has its last two electrons in separate degenerate π orbitals with parallel spins, so it is paramagnetic. N₂, C₂ and F₂ have all electrons paired.

quiz.q: Shortest bond among O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻, O₂²⁻:
quiz.why: Bond length falls as bond order rises. O₂⁺ has bond order 2.5, higher than O₂ (2), O₂⁻ (1.5) and O₂²⁻ (1), so it has the shortest bond.

quiz.q: He₂ is not stable because bond order is:
quiz.why: He₂ would have 2 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons, so bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0. With no net bonding it is not stable.
s–p mixing occurs when the 2s–2p energy gap is small, as in lighter diatomics like B₂, C₂ and N₂. For N₂ it places σ2p above π2p; O₂ and F₂ lack this.

questions.q: Quantum number deciding orbital shape:
questions.why: The azimuthal quantum number l determines the shape of an orbital (0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d). n gives size and energy; mₗ gives orientation.

questions.q: Hybridisation of C in CH₄:
questions.why: Carbon in CH₄ has four bond pairs, i.e. four electron domains, so it is sp³ hybridised with tetrahedral geometry.

questions.q: Bond order of N₂:
questions.why: N₂ has 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons: bond order = (10 − 4)/2 = 3, matching the triple bond.

questions.q: Total nodes in a 4f orbital:
questions.why: Total nodes = n − 1 = 3 for n = 4. Of these, l = 3 are angular and n − l − 1 = 0 are radial.

questions.q: Shape of XeF₄:
questions.why: XeF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs (steric number 6). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving a square planar shape.

questions.q: Cu⁺ salts are more covalent than Na⁺ salts mainly because Cu⁺:
questions.why: Cu⁺ has a pseudo-noble-gas 18-electron shell. The d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so Cu⁺ polarises anions strongly and its salts are more covalent than Na⁺ salts.

questions.q: Unpaired electrons in Fe³⁺:
questions.why: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. Five d electrons occupy five orbitals singly, giving 5 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Assertion: NH₃ has a smaller bond angle than CH₄. Reason: Lone pair–bond pair repulsion exceeds bond pair–bond pair repulsion.
questions.why: Both statements are true: NH₃ has one lone pair, and lone pair–bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair–bond pair, so its angle is smaller than CH₄'s. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Shape of I₃⁻:
questions.why: I₃⁻ has a central I with 2 bonds and 3 lone pairs (steric number 5). The three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, leaving a linear shape.

questions.q: Using Slater's rules, Zeff for a 2p electron of N (Z = 7):
questions.why: For a 2p electron in N: same-group electrons (4 others at 2s2p) contribute 0.35 each = 1.40 for 4... the given working S = 3.10 and Zeff = Z − S = 7 − 3.10 = 3.90.

questions.q: Case: For MgO, ΔH_sub = 148, IE₁ + IE₂ = 2188, ½D = 249, EA₁ + EA₂ = +603 (net), ΔH_f = −602 kJ/mol. Lattice energy:
Which species has bond order 2.5 and is paramagnetic?
questions.why: NO has 15 electrons: 10 bonding and 5 antibonding, so bond order = 2.5. The last electron is a single unpaired electron in π*, so it is paramagnetic. N₂, CO and CN⁻ are diamagnetic.

questions.q: Which pair are isostructural?
questions.why: XeF₂ and I₃⁻ both have steric number 5 with three lone pairs on the central atom, giving a linear shape. The other pairs differ in shape.

questions.q: Arrange in increasing bond length: O₂²⁻, O₂⁻, O₂, O₂⁺
questions.why: Bond order: O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂ 2, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1. Higher bond order means a shorter bond, so length increases as O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻.

questions.q: C₂ in its ground state (with s–p mixing) is:
questions.why: With s–p mixing C₂ fills π2p⁴ with σ2p empty. Bond order = (6 − 2)/2 = 2, and all electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic.

courses.title: Organic I · Electronic effects, intermediates, stereochemistry
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects on acidity and basicity, carbocations and other intermediates, chirality with R/S and E/Z, and SN1/SN2/E1/E2 mechanisms.
outcomes: Learners can rank acids and bases using electronic effects
Learners can predict carbocation stability and rearrangements
Learners can assign R/S and E/Z and identify meso compounds
Learners can choose between SN1, SN2, E1 and E2

scenes.text: Neha wonders why chloroacetic acid, used in labs, is far more acidic than the acetic acid in vinegar.
The chlorine pulls electron density away and stabilises the anion — the inductive effect.

steps.title: Three electronic effects
steps.body:
- **Inductive (I)**: polarisation through σ bonds, fades with distance. −I: NO₂ > CN > F > Cl > Br > I > OH; +I: alkyl groups.
- **Resonance (R/M)**: delocalisation through π systems. +R: −OH, −OR, −NH₂ (lone pair donors); −R: −NO₂, −C=O, −CN.
- **Hyperconjugation**: σ(C–H) → empty p or π* donation; explains why more substituted alkenes and carbocations are more stable.

Rule: anything that stabilises the conjugate base increases acidity.

steps.title: Solved: ranking acids
steps.body:
- ClCH₂COOH (pKa ≈ 2.9) > CH₃COOH (≈ 4.8): −I of Cl
- Cl₃CCOOH is stronger still (three −I groups)
- Phenol (pKa ≈ 10) ≫ ethanol (≈ 16): phenoxide is resonance stabilised
- p-Nitrophenol (≈ 7.2) > phenol: −R of NO₂ delocalises the negative charge further

steps.title: Solved: ranking bases
steps.body:
- Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than aniline: in aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
- In water, the usual order is (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃ — a balance of +I effects, solvation and steric hindrance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking −OH is only electron-withdrawing; on a benzene ring its +R dominates for ortho/para activation.
- Forgetting that inductive effects weaken quickly beyond 2–3 bonds.
- Comparing acidity by the acid's stability instead of the conjugate base's.
- Predicting gas-phase basicity order for amines in water.

activity.prompt: Arrange from MOST acidic to LEAST acidic.
items: Trichloroacetic acid
Chloroacetic acid
Acetic acid
Phenol
Ethanol

quiz.why: −NH₂ has a lone pair on N that it donates into a conjugated system (+R effect). −CHO, −NO₂ and −CN withdraw electrons (−R).

quiz.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
options: phenol is aromatic so no reason
quiz.why: The phenoxide ion's negative charge is delocalised into the ring by resonance, making it stabler than ethoxide, so phenol loses H⁺ more easily.
Hyperconjugation is delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond next to a π bond, a radical or a positive carbon. It is sometimes called no-bond resonance.
In aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton. The alkylamines and ammonia are more basic.
Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen and has the strongest −I effect, which stabilises the carboxylate and makes FCH₂COOH the strongest acid.

scenes.text: In practical class, Om adds HCl to 3-methylbut-1-ene and expects 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. The major product is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.
The carbocation rearranged by a hydride shift to a more stable tertiary cation.

steps.title: Four intermediates
steps.body:
- **Carbocations** (sp², planar, empty p): stability 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺; allyl and benzyl are resonance stabilised. They rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl shifts toward greater stability.
- **Carbanions** (usually sp³, pyramidal): stability order opposite to carbocations — CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3°; stabilised by −I/−R groups.
- **Free radicals** (≈ planar, 7 electrons): 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃•; allyl/benzyl extra stable.
- **Carbenes** (:CR₂): singlet (paired, sp²) or triplet (two unpaired).

steps.title: Solved: the hydride shift
steps.body:
3-methylbut-1-ene + H⁺ → secondary cation at C2.

- A hydride on C3 shifts to C2
- Positive charge moves to C3 — now tertiary
- Cl⁻ attacks → **2-chloro-2-methylbutane** (major)

steps.title: Solved: ranking cation stability
steps.body:
Benzyl ≈ allyl (resonance) vs tert-butyl:

- (C₆H₅)₃C⁺ > (C₆H₅)₂CH⁺ > C₆H₅CH₂⁺ — more rings, more delocalisation
- CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ (allyl) > CH₃CH₂⁺ (primary) by resonance
- A cation α to an electron-withdrawing group (e.g. next to C=O) is destabilised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying carbocation order to carbanions.
- Forgetting rearrangements in SN1/E1 and acid-catalysed additions.
- Drawing carbocations as tetrahedral (they are planar, which is why SN1 racemises).
- Thinking free radicals carry a charge.

activity.prompt: Most stable or least stable within its own class?

quiz.q: Hybridisation of carbon in a carbocation:
quiz.why: A carbocation carbon has three sigma bonds in a plane and an empty p orbital, so it is sp² hybridised and trigonal planar.
Alkyl groups donate electrons (+I), which intensifies the negative charge and destabilises carbanions. So the methyl carbanion with no alkyl groups is the most stable.

quiz.q: Benzyl cation is stable because of:
quiz.why: The benzyl cation's positive charge is delocalised over the ring through resonance, which makes it much more stable than simple primary cations.
Carbocations rearrange by 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl (methyl) shifts to form a more stable cation, e.g. secondary to tertiary.
A triplet carbene has two unpaired electrons with parallel spins in different orbitals, so it behaves as a diradical. A singlet carbene has paired electrons.

scenes.text: Farah tries to put her left glove on her right hand. Mirror images that cannot be superimposed — chirality.
Many drugs are chiral, and the two mirror forms can act differently in the body. Naming them correctly matters.

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Chiral**: not superimposable on its mirror image; commonly a carbon with four different groups (stereocentre)
- **Enantiomers**: non-superimposable mirror images; same physical properties except the direction of rotating plane-polarised light
- **Diastereomers**: stereoisomers that are not mirror images; different physical properties
- **Meso**: has stereocentres but an internal plane of symmetry → achiral (meso-tartaric acid)
- Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ for n stereocentres (fewer if meso forms exist)
- Specific rotation [α] = α/(l × c), l in dm, c in g/mL

steps.title: CIP priority rules
steps.body:
1. Higher atomic number at the first point of difference gets higher priority.
2. If tied, move outward to the next atoms and compare sets.
3. Double bonds count as duplicated atoms.

**R/S**: point the lowest priority (4) away; 1 → 2 → 3 clockwise = R, anticlockwise = S. If 4 points toward you, reverse the answer.
**E/Z**: higher-priority groups on the same side = Z (zusammen), opposite = E (entgegen).

steps.title: Solved: counting stereoisomers
steps.body:
- 2,3-Dibromobutane: 2 stereocentres → 2² = 4 expected, but (2R,3S) is meso → only **3** stereoisomers (a pair of enantiomers + meso)
- 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane: 4 stereoisomers (no meso; ends differ)

steps.title: Solved: specific rotation and ee
steps.body:
A solution of 0.5 g/mL in a 1 dm tube rotates light +6.65°.

- [α] = 6.65/(1 × 0.5) = **+13.3°**
- If the pure enantiomer has [α] = +19.0°, enantiomeric excess = 13.3/19.0 × 100 = **70% ee** (85 : 15 mixture)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming R means (+) rotation — the R/S label and sign of rotation are unrelated.
- Forgetting to reverse when the lowest-priority group points toward you.
- Using cis/trans when E/Z is needed for tri- or tetra-substituted alkenes.
- Counting 2ⁿ isomers without checking for meso forms.

statements.s: A meso compound is optically inactive.
Enantiomers have different boiling points.
statements.why: Identical physical properties in an achiral environment.

statements.s: A racemic mixture shows zero net optical rotation.
An (R) compound always rotates light clockwise.
Diastereomers can be separated by ordinary distillation or crystallisation.

quiz.q: Number of stereoisomers of tartaric acid:
quiz.why: Tartaric acid has two stereocentres but is symmetric, so there are d, l and meso forms: 3 stereoisomers (not 4).
CIP priority goes by atomic number of the atom directly attached: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1), so −OH ranks highest.
Enantiomers have identical physical properties except that they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

quiz.q: If the lowest-priority group points toward the viewer and the sequence looks clockwise, the configuration is:
quiz.why: If the lowest-priority group faces the viewer, the apparent direction is reversed. A clockwise sequence would look R, but really it is S.

quiz.q: Specific rotation when α = −4°, l = 2 dm, c = 0.1 g/mL:
quiz.why: Specific rotation = α/(l × c) = −4/(2 × 0.1) = −20°.

lessons.title: Substitution and elimination: SN1, SN2, E1, E2

scenes.text: Two students treat 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with different reagents: one with water, one with hot ethanolic KOH.
One gets an alcohol (substitution); the other an alkene (elimination). Substrate, nucleophile/base, solvent and temperature decide.

steps.title: The four mechanisms
steps.body:
- **SN2**: one step, backside attack, rate = k[RX][Nu], **inversion** (Walden). Fastest for CH₃ > 1° > 2°; 3° essentially no. Favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMSO, DMF).
- **SN1**: two steps via carbocation, rate = k[RX], **racemisation** (often with some inversion), possible rearrangement. 3° > 2°; polar protic solvents.
- **E2**: one step, strong base, **anti-periplanar** H and leaving group; usually **Zaitsev** (more substituted alkene), but bulky bases (t-BuO⁻) favour Hofmann (less substituted).
- **E1**: via carbocation, competes with SN1, favoured by heat.

steps.title: Solved: predicting the product
steps.body:
- (R)-2-bromobutane + NaI in acetone → **(S)-2-iodobutane** (SN2, inversion; Finkelstein)
- (CH₃)₃CBr in water/ethanol, warm → (CH₃)₃COH via SN1 (+ some alkene by E1)
- (CH₃)₃CBr + hot alcoholic KOH → **2-methylpropene** (E2)

steps.title: Solved: Zaitsev vs Hofmann
steps.body:
2-Bromobutane + base:

- Ethoxide (small) → but-2-ene major (more substituted, Zaitsev)
- tert-Butoxide (bulky) → but-1-ene proportion rises (Hofmann product), because the base reaches the less hindered H more easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Proposing SN2 at a tertiary carbon.
- Forgetting that SN1 gives (near) racemisation, not retention.
- Ignoring rearrangement possibilities in SN1/E1.
- Using a polar protic solvent to speed up SN2 (it solvates and slows the nucleophile).

a.text: Substrate: 1-bromobutane. Reagent: NaCN in DMSO. Which pathway dominates?

choices.label: SN2
choices.feedback: Yes — primary substrate, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent.

choices.label: SN1
choices.feedback: A primary carbocation is too unstable.

a2.text: Think again: 1° substrates rarely ionise. Choose again.

b.text: Next: tert-butyl bromide in hot ethanolic KOH. Main pathway?

choices.label: E2
choices.feedback: Right — strong base, tertiary substrate, heat → elimination.

choices.label: SN2
choices.feedback: Backside attack is blocked at a 3° carbon.

b2.text: Tertiary carbons do not undergo SN2. Try again.

end.text: Rule of thumb: look at substrate class, then reagent strength/bulk, then solvent and temperature.

quiz.why: SN2 involves backside attack by the nucleophile, so the configuration at the carbon is inverted (Walden inversion).
SN1 is unimolecular: the slow ionisation of RX to a carbocation is rate-determining, so rate = k[RX], independent of the nucleophile.

quiz.q: E2 requires the H and leaving group to be:
quiz.why: E2 is a one-step elimination needing the H and leaving group to be anti-periplanar so the orbitals overlap well as the π bond forms.
Polar aprotic solvents like DMSO solvate cations but not the nucleophile, leaving it 'naked' and reactive, which suits SN2. Protic solvents hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile.
A bulky base cannot reach the more hindered hydrogen, so it removes the less hindered one and gives the less substituted alkene (Hofmann product).

questions.q: −NO₂ shows:
questions.why: −NO₂ strongly withdraws electrons both through sigma bonds (−I) and by resonance (−R), making it a strong electron-withdrawing group.

questions.q: A carbon with four different groups is a:
questions.why: A carbon bonded to four different groups is a stereocentre (chiral centre) and can give enantiomers.

questions.q: Most stable carbocation:
questions.why: Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by three alkyl groups through +I and hyperconjugation, so they are more stable than secondary, primary and methyl.

questions.q: Racemic mixture rotation:
questions.why: A racemic mixture holds equal amounts of both enantiomers, and their rotations cancel, giving zero net rotation.

questions.q: Higher priority between −CH₂OH and −CH(CH₃)₂:
questions.why: Both carbons at the first point tie (C vs C). At the next set, −CH₂OH has (O, H, H) against (C, C, H), and O beats C, so −CH₂OH has higher priority.

questions.q: Aniline is less basic than methylamine due to:
questions.why: In aniline the N lone pair is delocalised into the ring by resonance, so it is less able to take up a proton than in methylamine, where +I raises basicity.

questions.q: Assertion: SN1 at a chiral centre gives mostly racemic product. Reason: The carbocation is planar and attacked from both faces.
questions.why: Both are true: SN1 proceeds via a planar carbocation attacked from either face, giving a mostly racemic mixture. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Number of stereoisomers of 2,3-dichlorobutane:
questions.why: 2,3-Dichlorobutane has two stereocentres, so 2² = 4 would be expected, but one form is meso, so only 3 stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers and the meso form.

questions.q: Strongest acid:
questions.why: The nitro group at the para position withdraws electrons by −R, stabilising the phenoxide, so p-nitrophenol is the strongest acid. Methyl and methoxy donate electrons and weaken acidity.

questions.q: (S)-2-chlorobutane with NaSH in DMF gives:
questions.why: SH⁻ in the polar aprotic DMF gives an SN2 reaction, with inversion of configuration. Since priorities of the groups keep the same order, (S) becomes (R)-butane-2-thiol.

questions.q: Case: A sample of an enantiomer with [α]pure = +40° shows [α]obs = +10°. Percentage of the (+) form:
questions.why: Optical purity = 10/40 = 25% ee. The remainder 75% is racemic, 37.5% each, so (+) = 25 + 37.5 = 62.5%.

questions.q: Major product when 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene reacts with HBr:
questions.why: H⁺ adds to the terminal CH₂ to give a secondary cation, which undergoes a methyl shift to a tertiary cation. Br⁻ then attacks to give 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.q: Which conformation is required for E2 in a cyclohexyl halide?
options: axial leaving group with axial anti H
questions.why: E2 in cyclohexane requires the leaving group and the β-hydrogen to be trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar), so the leaving group must be axial with an axial anti H.

questions.q: Rank SN2 rates: CH₃Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr, CH₃CH₂Br, (CH₃)₃CBr
questions.why: SN2 rate falls as steric hindrance at the carbon increases: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary (which essentially does not react by SN2).

questions.q: Which statement on carbenes is correct?
options: Singlet carbenes add to cis-alkenes stereospecifically
Carbenes have 8 valence electrons on C
questions.why: Singlet carbenes (paired electrons) add in a concerted, stereospecific step, so cis alkene gives cis cyclopropane. Triplet carbenes react stepwise, and carbene carbon has 6, not 8, electrons.

courses.title: Physical I · Chemical thermodynamics and kinetics
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Thermochemistry with Hess and Kirchhoff, Gibbs energy and equilibrium, rate laws and integrated equations, and Arrhenius behaviour with collision and transition-state ideas.
outcomes: Learners can relate ΔH and ΔU and apply Hess's law
Learners can predict spontaneity and K from ΔG°
Learners can use integrated rate laws and half-lives
Learners can compute activation energy from rate data

lessons.title: Thermochemistry: ΔH, ΔU, Hess and Kirchhoff

scenes.text: Ananya wonders how much heat her family's LPG cylinder really gives.
Enthalpies of combustion and Hess's law answer it without burning anything in a calorimeter twice.

steps.title: Core relations
steps.body:
- ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT (Δn_g = moles of gaseous products − reactants)
- **Hess's law**: ΔH of a reaction is the same however it is carried out (state function)
- From formation enthalpies: ΔH° = ΣΔH_f°(products) − ΣΔH_f°(reactants)
- From bond enthalpies (gas phase, approximate): ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
- **Kirchhoff**: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔC_p (T₂ − T₁)

steps.title: Solved: Hess's law
steps.body:
Given C + O₂ → CO₂ (−393.5 kJ) and CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ (−283.0 kJ). Find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO.

- Reverse the second: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂ (+283.0)
- Add to the first: C + ½O₂ → CO
- ΔH = −393.5 + 283.0 = **−110.5 kJ**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting liquids/solids in Δn_g.
- Mixing J and kJ when using R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
- Forgetting to multiply ΔH when scaling equations.
- Using bond enthalpies for liquids (they are gas-phase averages).

activity.prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.4 kJ at 298 K. Find ΔU in kJ (R = 8.314 J/mol K).

quiz.q: Hess's law follows because enthalpy is a:
quiz.why: Enthalpy is a state function, depending only on initial and final states, so the total change is the same by any route. That is Hess's law.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. When Δn_g = 0 the PV work term vanishes, so ΔH = ΔU.
Kirchhoff's equation gives how ΔH changes with temperature: ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ = ΔC_p (T₂ − T₁).

quiz.q: Standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state:
quiz.why: By definition, the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable standard state is zero, since it is the reference point.

quiz.q: ΔH for 2C + O₂ → 2CO using the example data:
quiz.why: Forming 1 mol CO releases 110.5 kJ; the equation makes 2 mol CO, so ΔH = 2 × (−110.5) = −221 kJ.

story.title: Ice melts on its own — only when warm

scenes.text: Melting absorbs heat (ΔH > 0), yet ice melts by itself on a warm day.
Entropy increase wins above 0 °C. Gibbs energy balances both.

steps.title: The Gibbs criterion
steps.body:
- At constant T and P: **ΔG = ΔH − TΔS**; ΔG < 0 spontaneous, ΔG = 0 equilibrium
- ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; at equilibrium ΔG° = −RT ln K
- Link to cells: ΔG° = −nFE°
- Sign table: ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0 → always spontaneous; ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0 → never; mixed signs → depends on T (crossover T = ΔH/ΔS)

steps.title: Solved: crossover temperature
steps.body:
ΔH = +40 kJ/mol, ΔS = +100 J/mol K.

- T = ΔH/ΔS = 40000/100 = **400 K**
- Spontaneous above 400 K, non-spontaneous below.

steps.title: Solved: K from ΔG°
steps.body:
ΔG° = −10.0 kJ/mol at 298 K.

- ln K = −ΔG°/RT = 10000/(8.314 × 298) = 4.04
- K = e^4.04 ≈ **57**
- A ΔG° of −5.7 kJ corresponds to roughly a tenfold K at 298 K (2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ΔG° (standard) to judge spontaneity under non-standard conditions — use ΔG.
- Mixing kJ (ΔH) and J (ΔS).
- Thinking spontaneous means fast (kinetics is separate).
- Forgetting that ln K needs natural log, or use log K = −ΔG°/(2.303RT).

activity.prompt: Classify each case at all temperatures.

quiz.why: At equilibrium the system has no tendency to change, so ΔG = 0. ΔG° equals −RT ln K and is not zero in general.
ΔG° = −RT ln K. If K > 1, ln K is positive, so ΔG° is negative.
ΔG° = −nFE° links free energy to cell potential, so it connects thermodynamics to electrochemistry.

quiz.q: ΔH = −20 kJ, ΔS = −50 J/K. Spontaneous below:
quiz.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 needs −20000 + 50T < 0, i.e. T < 20000/50 = 400 K. Spontaneous below 400 K.
The general criterion for spontaneity at constant T and P is ΔG < 0. Exothermic reactions are not always spontaneous, and spontaneity says nothing about speed.

scenes.text: A pharmacist explains that a medicine is discarded after it loses 10% of its strength.
Drug decomposition often follows first-order kinetics, so its shelf life can be calculated.

steps.title: Order and integrated forms
steps.body:
Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; order = m + n (found experimentally). Molecularity is the number of species in an elementary step (whole number, ≤ 3).

- **Zero order**: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; t½ = [A]₀/2k
- **First order**: ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt, or k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]); t½ = 0.693/k (independent of [A]₀)
- **Second order** (one reactant): 1/[A] − 1/[A]₀ = kt; t½ = 1/(k[A]₀)
- **Pseudo-first order**: one reactant in large excess (e.g. acid hydrolysis of ester in water)
- Units of k: zero mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, first s⁻¹, second L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

steps.title: Solved: half-lives
steps.body:
First-order reaction with t½ = 10 min.

- Time for 87.5% completion: remaining 12.5% = (½)³ ⇒ **30 min**
- k = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 min⁻¹
- Time for 99.9%: t = (2.303/k) log 1000 ≈ 10 half-lives ≈ **100 min**

steps.title: Solved: shelf life
steps.body:
A drug decomposes first order with k = 0.005 day⁻¹. Shelf life t₉₀ (10% lost)?

- t = (2.303/0.005) log(100/90) = 460.6 × 0.0458 ≈ **21 days**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading order from the balanced equation (only valid for elementary steps).
- Using t½ = 0.693/k for non-first-order reactions.
- Mixing log and ln (2.303 factor).
- Forgetting that molecularity can't be zero or fractional; order can.

activity.prompt: A first-order reaction is 75% complete in 40 minutes. What is its half-life in minutes?

quiz.why: For first order, t½ = 0.693/k, which has no [A]₀ term, so it is independent of initial concentration.

quiz.q: Units of k for second-order reaction:
quiz.why: For second order, rate = k[A]², so k has units (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)/(mol L⁻¹)² = L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate is typically:
quiz.why: In acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, water is in huge excess and its concentration is effectively constant, so the reaction behaves as pseudo-first order.

quiz.q: For zero order, a plot of [A] vs t is:
quiz.why: For zero order, [A] = [A]₀ − kt, which is a straight line with slope −k.
Each half-life halves the amount: (½)⁴ = 1/16 is left after 4 half-lives.

story.title: Why the fridge keeps milk fresh

scenes.text: Milk left out sours in a day; in the fridge it lasts several days.
Bacterial and chemical reaction rates drop sharply with temperature, as Arrhenius described.

steps.title: Arrhenius equation
steps.body:
- k = A e^(−Ea/RT); ln k = ln A − Ea/RT (plot ln k vs 1/T: slope −Ea/R)
- Two temperatures: **log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)**
- Rough rule near room temperature: rate doubles or triples per 10 K
- **Collision theory**: rate = Z × e^(−Ea/RT) × p (steric factor)
- **Transition state theory**: activated complex at the top of the energy barrier
- A catalyst lowers Ea by providing an alternative path; it does not change ΔH, ΔG or K

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Arrhenius.
- Ea in kJ with R in J (convert!).
- Believing catalysts shift equilibrium.
- Mixing sign: 1/T₁ − 1/T₂ is positive when T₂ > T₁.

activity.label: Activation energy (kJ/mol) — how sensitive is the rate to a 10 K rise near 300 K?

bands.text: Low Ea: rate rises only ~1.3–1.5× per 10 K.
Moderate Ea: about 2× per 10 K — the classic rule of thumb.
Very high Ea: rate is extremely temperature-sensitive (~7× or more per 10 K).

quiz.why: From the Arrhenius equation ln k = ln A − Ea/RT, a plot of ln k against 1/T has slope −Ea/R. The 2.303 appears only with log₁₀.
A catalyst offers an alternative pathway with lower activation energy Ea. It leaves ΔG, ΔH and K unchanged.

quiz.q: Units of A for a first-order reaction:
quiz.why: In k = A e^(−Ea/RT) the exponential is unitless, so A has the same units as k; for first order that is s⁻¹.
The steric (orientation) factor p allows for the fact that only collisions with proper orientation lead to reaction.
Since k depends exponentially on −Ea/RT, a larger Ea makes the rate change more steeply with temperature.

questions.q: Unit of rate constant for a first-order reaction:
questions.why: For first order, k = rate/[A], so units are (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)/(mol L⁻¹) = s⁻¹.

questions.q: Enthalpy is a:
questions.why: Enthalpy depends only on the state of the system, not on the path, so it is a state function. That is the basis of Hess's law.

questions.q: A catalyst does NOT change:
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it changes the rate and the Ea path but not the equilibrium constant.

questions.q: ΔG° for a reaction with K = 1:
questions.why: ΔG° = −RT ln K. If K = 1, ln K = 0, so ΔG° = 0.

questions.q: Time for 75% completion of a first-order reaction equals:
questions.why: 75% completion means 25% is left, which is (½)² so 2 half-lives are needed: 2 t½.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g), ΔH and ΔU are:
questions.why: Moles of gas are 2 on both sides, so Δn_g = 0. Then ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT = ΔU.

questions.q: Assertion: The order of a reaction can be fractional. Reason: Order is determined experimentally and may reflect a complex mechanism.
questions.why: Both statements are true: order is found by experiment and can be fractional for complex mechanisms, such as 3/2. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: ΔH = +30 kJ, ΔS = +75 J/K. Minimum T for spontaneity:
questions.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS ≤ 0 needs T ≥ ΔH/ΔS = 30000/75 = 400 K.

questions.q: Second-order reaction with k = 0.5 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ and [A]₀ = 0.2 M has t½:
questions.why: For second order, t½ = 1/(k[A]₀) = 1/(0.5 × 0.2) = 1/0.1 = 10 s.

questions.q: Case: Data — ΔH_f(CO₂) = −393.5, ΔH_f(H₂O, l) = −285.8, ΔH_f(C₂H₅OH, l) = −277.7 kJ/mol. ΔH_combustion of ethanol:
Ea = 60 kJ/mol. Ratio k(310 K)/k(300 K) ≈:
ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol at 298 K gives K ≈:
A first-order reaction has k = 2.31 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Time to fall to 1/10 of initial:
questions.why: For first order t = (2.303/k) log([A]₀/[A]) with ratio 10: t = 2.303/(2.31 × 10⁻³) ≈ 997 s ≈ 1000 s.

questions.q: For a reaction, ΔH(298 K) = −100 kJ and ΔC_p = +20 J/K. ΔH at 398 K:
questions.why: Kirchhoff: ΔH₂ = ΔH₁ + ΔC_p ΔT = −100 kJ + 0.020 kJ/K × 100 K = −100 + 2 = −98 kJ.

questions.q: For A → products, doubling [A] increases rate by factor 2√2. Order:
questions.why: Rate ∝ [A]ⁿ, so doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 2ⁿ. Since 2√2 = 2^1.5, n = 1.5.

courses.title: Physical II · Electrochemistry and ionic equilibria
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Conductance and Kohlrausch's law, galvanic cells and the Nernst equation, pH, buffers and solubility product, and electrolysis with Faraday's laws.
outcomes: Learners can calculate molar conductivity and degree of dissociation
Learners can compute cell EMF, ΔG° and K
Learners can find pH of weak acids and buffers and use Ksp
Learners can apply Faraday's laws

scenes.text: A water purifier technician dips a TDS/conductivity probe in tap water and then in RO water.
Ions carry current; fewer ions, lower conductance. Chemists quantify this with molar conductivity.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Conductance G = 1/R (S); conductivity κ = G × (l/A), l/A = cell constant
- Molar conductivity Λm = κ × 1000/c (S cm² mol⁻¹ with κ in S cm⁻¹, c in mol L⁻¹)
- Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λm° − A√c (Debye–Hückel–Onsager)
- Weak electrolytes: Λm rises steeply on dilution; α = Λm/Λm°; Ka = cα²/(1 − α)
- **Kohlrausch's law**: Λm° = ν₊λ₊° + ν₋λ₋° (independent migration of ions)

steps.title: Solved: Λm° of a weak acid
steps.body:
Λm°(CH₃COOH) cannot be found by extrapolation. Use strong electrolytes (S cm² mol⁻¹):

- Λ°(HCl) = 426.2, Λ°(CH₃COONa) = 91.0, Λ°(NaCl) = 126.5
- Λ°(CH₃COOH) = 426.2 + 91.0 − 126.5 = **390.7**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1000 factor (L to cm³).
- Extrapolating weak-electrolyte Λm to zero concentration.
- Confusing conductivity (κ) and conductance (G).
- Thinking conductivity rises on dilution — κ falls; Λm rises.

activity.prompt: A cell has constant 1.2 cm⁻¹ and resistance 400 Ω with 0.01 M KCl. Molar conductivity in S cm² mol⁻¹?

quiz.why: Kohlrausch's law says that at infinite dilution each ion migrates independently, so the limiting molar conductivity is the sum of the ionic contributions.

quiz.q: On dilution, conductivity κ of a solution:
quiz.why: Conductivity κ is conductance per unit volume, which depends on the number of ions per unit volume. On dilution there are fewer ions per cm³, so κ decreases.

quiz.q: On dilution, Λm of a weak electrolyte:
quiz.why: For a weak electrolyte, dilution increases the degree of dissociation α sharply, giving more ions, so Λm rises steeply at low concentration.
Cell constant = l/A, length divided by area, so its unit is cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: α = 0.1 for 0.01 M weak acid. Ka:
quiz.why: Ka = Cα²/(1 − α) = 0.01 × 0.01/0.9 = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴. Ignoring the (1 − α) term would give 1 × 10⁻⁴.

lessons.title: Galvanic cells and the Nernst equation

scenes.text: Kids push copper and zinc strips into a lemon and light a tiny LED with a few lemons in series.
Each Zn–Cu pair is a galvanic cell. Its voltage depends on standard potentials and on concentrations — Nernst.

steps.title: Cells and potentials
steps.body:
- Anode: oxidation (− in galvanic); cathode: reduction (+)
- E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), using standard reduction potentials vs SHE (0.00 V)
- **Nernst** (298 K): E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q
- ΔG° = −nFE° (F = 96485 C/mol); log K = nE°/0.0591
- Concentration cells: E° = 0; EMF from concentration difference alone

steps.title: Solved: equilibrium constant
steps.body:
For the same cell, log K = 2 × 1.10/0.0591 = 37.2.

- K ≈ **1.6 × 10³⁷** — the reaction goes essentially to completion.
- Concentration cell Cu | Cu²⁺(0.01) || Cu²⁺(1.0) | Cu: E = (0.0591/2) log 100 = **0.059 V**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying E° by stoichiometric coefficients (E° is intensive — never multiply).
- Putting solids or pure liquids into Q.
- Using E°anode as an oxidation potential and then subtracting again (double sign flip).
- Forgetting n in the Nernst equation.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to calculate the EMF of a cell at non-standard conditions.
items: Identify anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction)
Write the balanced overall reaction and n
Compute E° = E°cathode − E°anode
Write Q from concentrations (exclude solids)
Apply E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q

quiz.q: In a galvanic cell, the anode is:
quiz.why: At the anode of a galvanic cell oxidation occurs and electrons are released, so it is the negative terminal.
The standard hydrogen electrode is defined as the reference and has E° = 0.00 V at all temperatures.
ΔG° = −nFE°. A positive E°cell makes ΔG° negative, meaning the reaction is spontaneous.
A concentration cell has identical electrodes, so E°cell = 0. Its EMF comes only from the concentration difference.

quiz.q: For Cu²⁺/Cu (E° = 0.34 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (0.80 V), E°cell:
quiz.why: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − 0.34 = 0.46 V, with Ag⁺/Ag as the cathode.

scenes.text: A physiology student learns that blood pH is held close to 7.4 despite acids from metabolism.
Buffer systems such as carbonic acid/bicarbonate absorb the shock — the Henderson equation shows how.

steps.title: Key relations (25 °C)
steps.body:
- Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; pH + pOH = 14
- Weak acid (α small): [H⁺] = √(Ka c); pH = ½(pKa − log c)
- **Henderson–Hasselbalch**: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); best buffering within pKa ± 1
- Salt of weak acid + strong base: basic (hydrolysis); pH = 7 + ½(pKa + log c)
- **Ksp**: for AB, Ksp = s²; for AB₂, Ksp = 4s³. Common-ion effect lowers solubility; precipitation when ionic product > Ksp

steps.title: Solved: Ksp and common ion
steps.body:
AgCl, Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰.

- In water: s = √Ksp = **1.34 × 10⁻⁵ M**
- In 0.1 M NaCl: s = Ksp/0.1 = **1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M** — about 7000 times lower

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using √(Ka c) when the acid is not weak or very dilute (check α < 5%).
- Forgetting stoichiometric factors in Ksp (e.g. 4s³).
- Taking the log ratio upside down in Henderson's equation.
- Assuming pH 7 is neutral at all temperatures (Kw changes with T).

activity.prompt: A buffer contains 0.05 M NH₄⁺ and 0.05 M NH₃ (pKb of NH₃ = 4.75). What is its pH?

quiz.why: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M and pH = 3.

quiz.q: A buffer works best when pH ≈:
quiz.why: By the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). A buffer is most effective when acid and base are equal, so pH ≈ pKa.

quiz.q: Ksp of CaF₂ in terms of s:
quiz.why: CaF₂ gives Ca²⁺ = s and F⁻ = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³.

quiz.q: Adding NaCl to saturated AgCl solution:
quiz.why: NaCl adds Cl⁻, the common ion, shifting AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the left, so AgCl solubility decreases.
Sodium acetate is a salt of a strong base and a weak acid. Acetate hydrolyses to give OH⁻, so the solution is basic.

lessons.title: Electrolysis, Faraday's laws, batteries and corrosion

scenes.text: A visit to an electroplating unit shows taps coated with chromium and nickel.
How thick the coat is depends on current and time — Faraday's laws, used daily in industry.

steps.title: Faraday's laws
steps.body:
- First law: mass deposited m = Z I t, with Z = M/(nF)
- Second law: for the same charge, masses deposited are proportional to equivalent masses (M/n)
- 1 F = 96485 C ≈ charge on 1 mol electrons

Products depend on electrode potentials and overpotential: electrolysis of aqueous NaCl gives H₂ at cathode and Cl₂ at anode (concentrated brine), not Na.

steps.title: Solved: copper plating
steps.body:
2 A for 965 s through CuSO₄.

- Q = 1930 C = 0.02 F
- Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu: moles Cu = 0.01
- Mass = 0.01 × 63.5 = **0.635 g**

steps.title: Solved: aluminium
steps.body:
How many coulombs to produce 27 g of Al from Al³⁺?

- 1 mol Al needs 3 mol e⁻
- Q = 3 × 96485 ≈ **2.9 × 10⁵ C**
- This is why aluminium smelting is so electricity-intensive.

steps.title: Batteries and corrosion
steps.body:
- Lead–acid: Pb anode, PbO₂ cathode, H₂SO₄ electrolyte; rechargeable
- H₂–O₂ fuel cell: E° ≈ 1.23 V; product water
- Lithium-ion: Li⁺ shuttles between graphite and a metal-oxide cathode
- Rusting is an electrochemical cell on the iron surface; prevention by painting, galvanising (zinc coat) and sacrificial anodes (Mg/Zn blocks on ship hulls)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting n (charge on the ion).
- Using minutes instead of seconds.
- Predicting Na metal at the cathode in aqueous electrolysis.
- Thinking galvanising works only as a barrier (zinc also corrodes preferentially).

activity.prompt: What mass of silver (M = 108) is deposited by 1.0 A flowing for 1930 s through AgNO₃? (F = 96500 C)

quiz.why: One mole of electrons carries one faraday, F = 96485 C/mol (about 96500 C). 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the charge of one electron.

quiz.q: Same charge deposits masses proportional to:
quiz.why: Faraday's second law: masses deposited by the same charge are proportional to the equivalent masses of the substances.

quiz.q: Cathode product in electrolysis of aqueous NaCl:
quiz.why: In aqueous NaCl water is reduced more easily than Na⁺, so H₂ gas is released at the cathode.
Galvanised iron is coated with zinc, which is more reactive and corrodes in preference to iron (sacrificial protection).

quiz.q: Standard EMF of H₂–O₂ fuel cell:
quiz.why: The H₂–O₂ fuel cell's standard EMF is the E° of the O₂/H₂O couple, 1.23 V, as H⁺/H₂ is 0.

questions.q: SI unit of conductance:
questions.why: Conductance is the inverse of resistance (1/R), and its SI unit is the siemens (S). Ohm is the unit of resistance.

questions.q: pH of pure water at 25 °C:
questions.why: At 25 °C pure water has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M, so pH = 7 (neutral).

questions.q: Oxidation occurs at the:
questions.why: Oxidation always takes place at the anode, and reduction at the cathode, by definition.

questions.q: Purpose of a salt bridge:
questions.why: A salt bridge lets ions flow between the half-cells so charge does not build up, keeping each solution electrically neutral and the circuit complete.

questions.q: Solubility of Mg(OH)₂ is s. Ksp:
questions.why: Mg(OH)₂ ⇌ Mg²⁺ + 2OH⁻ gives [Mg²⁺] = s and [OH⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³.

questions.q: pH of 0.01 M NaOH:
questions.why: For 0.01 M NaOH, [OH⁻] = 10⁻², pOH = 2, so pH = 14 − 2 = 12.

questions.q: Assertion: Λm of a weak electrolyte cannot be extrapolated to infinite dilution. Reason: Its Λm rises steeply at low c.
questions.why: Both statements are true: the Λm of a weak electrolyte shoots up at low concentration, so the plot cannot be extrapolated to Λm°, and Kohlrausch's law is used instead. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: pH of 0.01 M weak acid with Ka = 1 × 10⁻⁶:
questions.why: For a weak acid [H⁺] = √(Ka·C) = √(10⁻⁶ × 10⁻²) = 10⁻⁴ M, so pH = 4.

questions.q: Mass of Cu deposited by 0.5 F:
questions.why: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu needs 2 F per mole, so 0.5 F deposits 0.25 mol. Mass = 0.25 × 63.5 ≈ 15.9 g.

questions.q: Case: Ni | Ni²⁺(0.01 M) || Ag⁺(0.1 M) | Ag; E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.25 V, E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = 0.80 V. EMF at 298 K:
Buffer of 0.1 M HA and 0.1 M A⁻ (pKa 4.74), 1 L; 0.01 mol HCl added. New pH:
Will AgCl precipitate when 10⁻⁴ M Ag⁺ meets 10⁻⁵ M Cl⁻ (Ksp 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰)?
questions.why: Ion product = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹, which is greater than Ksp (1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰), so AgCl precipitates.

questions.q: For a cell, E° = 0.59 V, n = 1. log K at 298 K:
Λ°(NH₄OH) from Λ°(NH₄Cl) = 129.8, Λ°(NaOH) = 248.1, Λ°(NaCl) = 126.4 (S cm² mol⁻¹):
questions.why: By Kohlrausch's law Λ°(NH₄OH) = Λ°(NH₄Cl) + Λ°(NaOH) − Λ°(NaCl) = 129.8 + 248.1 − 126.4 = 251.5.

questions.q: pH of 0.1 M sodium acetate (pKa 4.74):
questions.why: Acetate hydrolysis: pH = 7 + ½(pKa + log C) = 7 + ½(4.74 − 1) = 7 + 1.87 = 8.87. The solution is basic, so it must be above 7.

courses.title: Inorganic II · Coordination chemistry
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Werner's theory and IUPAC naming, structural and stereo-isomerism, crystal field theory with CFSE and magnetism, and colour, VBT, Jahn–Teller and applications.
outcomes: Learners can name complexes and interpret Werner's experiments
Learners can count geometric and optical isomers
Learners can predict spin state, CFSE and magnetic moment
Learners can explain colour and common applications of complexes

scenes.text: Werner noticed that CoCl₃·6NH₃ gave three moles of AgCl with silver nitrate, but CoCl₃·5NH₃ gave only two.
Some chlorides are bound directly to cobalt and some are not — the birth of coordination chemistry.

steps.title: Werner's postulates
steps.body:
- **Primary valency** = oxidation state (ionisable, satisfied by anions)
- **Secondary valency** = coordination number (non-ionisable, directed in space)
- [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃ → 3 Cl⁻ free; [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ → 2; [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl → 1

Ligands: monodentate (NH₃, Cl⁻, H₂O), bidentate (en, oxalate), hexadentate (EDTA⁴⁻); ambidentate (NO₂⁻/ONO⁻, SCN⁻/NCS⁻).

steps.title: IUPAC naming rules
steps.body:
1. Cation before anion.
2. Inside the sphere: ligands alphabetically (ignore prefixes di-, tri-), then metal.
3. Anionic ligands end in -o: chlorido, cyanido, oxalato; neutral: aqua, ammine, carbonyl.
4. Oxidation state in Roman numerals.
5. In an anionic complex the metal takes -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate).

steps.title: Solved: names
steps.body:
- K₄[Fe(CN)₆]: potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)
- [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
- [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]: diamminedichloridoplatinum(II)
- EAN of Fe in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: 26 − 2 + 12 = **36** (krypton configuration)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Alphabetising with prefixes (use 'ammine' under a, 'chlorido' under c).
- Forgetting -ate for anionic complexes.
- Mis-calculating oxidation state: sum of ligand charges + metal = complex charge.
- Spelling ammine (NH₃) as amine.

activity.prompt: Match the complex to its moles of AgCl precipitated per mole (excess AgNO₃).

quiz.why: Ethylenediamine (en) is bidentate, so three en ligands donate 3 × 2 = 6 donor atoms. Coordination number is 6.

quiz.q: Oxidation state of Fe in K₃[Fe(CN)₆]:
quiz.why: The complex ion carries −3 since there are three K⁺. With six CN⁻: x + 6(−1) = −3, so Fe is +3.

quiz.q: Name of NH₃ as a ligand:
quiz.why: In IUPAC nomenclature NH₃ as a ligand is called 'ammine' (double m), to distinguish it from organic amines.
SCN⁻ can bind through S (thiocyanato) or N (isothiocyanato), so it is ambidentate. NH₃ and H₂O are monodentate and en is bidentate.
In Werner's theory, primary valency is the oxidation state and secondary valency is the coordination number of the metal.

scenes.text: cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin) is a cancer drug; the trans isomer is far less useful.
Same atoms, different arrangement, different biology. That's geometric isomerism.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
**Structural**
- Ionisation: [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄ vs [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br
- Hydrate: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ vs [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O
- Linkage: –NO₂ (nitrito-N) vs –ONO (nitrito-O)
- Coordination: [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] vs [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆]

**Stereo**
- Geometric: square planar MA₂B₂ (cis/trans); octahedral MA₄B₂ (cis/trans), MA₃B₃ (fac/mer)
- Optical: octahedral complexes with chelates, e.g. [Co(en)₃]³⁺ (Δ/Λ), cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺
- Tetrahedral MA₂B₂ shows no geometric isomerism

steps.title: Solved: [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺
steps.body:
- trans: has a mirror plane → optically inactive (1 isomer)
- cis: no mirror plane → a pair of enantiomers (2)
- Total stereoisomers = **3**

steps.title: Solved: [Co(NH₃)₃Cl₃]
steps.body:
- fac: three Cl on one face (all mutually cis)
- mer: three Cl in a meridian (two trans)
- **2** geometric isomers, neither optically active.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assigning geometric isomers to tetrahedral MA₂B₂.
- Forgetting the cis isomer of [M(AA)₂B₂] is chiral.
- Treating ionisation and linkage isomerism as the same.
- Missing that square planar complexes with four different ligands give 3 geometric isomers.

items.back: 2 geometric isomers: cis and trans; neither chiral
Optically active: Δ and Λ enantiomers

quiz.why: In one, Br is inside the coordination sphere and SO₄²⁻ outside; in the other they are swapped. They give different ions in solution, so this is ionisation isomerism.
fac and mer isomers arise in octahedral complexes of type MA₃B₃, depending on whether the three like ligands lie on one face or a meridian.
cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ has no plane of symmetry and so exists as a non-superimposable mirror pair. The trans form is symmetric and thus inactive.
Linkage isomerism arises when an ambidentate ligand (such as NO₂⁻ or SCN⁻) can bind through different donor atoms.
Cisplatin is cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], with the two Cl on the same side. The trans isomer is not an effective drug.

lessons.title: Crystal field theory, CFSE and magnetism

scenes.text: In the lab, [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is attracted by a magnet strongly, but [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is not attracted at all.
Cyanide splits the d orbitals so widely that electrons pair up. Crystal field theory explains it.

steps.title: Octahedral splitting
steps.body:
Six ligands along the axes raise the d orbitals pointing at them.

- **e_g** (d_z², d_x²−y²): +0.6Δo
- **t₂g** (d_xy, d_yz, d_xz): −0.4Δo
- Tetrahedral: reversed and smaller, Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo → almost always high spin

**Spectrochemical series** (weak → strong field): I⁻ < Br⁻ < S²⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < NO₂⁻ < CN⁻ < CO.

For d⁴–d⁷: if Δo > P (pairing energy) → **low spin**; if Δo < P → **high spin**.

steps.title: CFSE and spin-only moment
steps.body:
- CFSE = (−0.4 × n_t₂g + 0.6 × n_eg)Δo (+ pairing terms if needed)
- Spin-only magnetic moment **μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM**, n = unpaired electrons: 1 → 1.73, 2 → 2.83, 3 → 3.87, 4 → 4.90, 5 → 5.92

steps.title: Solved: d⁶ high vs low spin
steps.body:
- [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻: Fe²⁺ d⁶, CN⁻ strong → t₂g⁶ e_g⁰, CFSE = −2.4Δo (+ pairing), **n = 0, diamagnetic**
- [CoF₆]³⁻: Co³⁺ d⁶, F⁻ weak → t₂g⁴ e_g², CFSE = −0.4Δo, **n = 4, μ = 4.90 BM**

steps.title: Solved: magnetic data to structure
steps.body:
[Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has μ ≈ 5.9 BM.

- √(n(n + 2)) = 5.9 ⇒ n = 5
- Mn²⁺ d⁵ high spin t₂g³ e_g², CFSE = 3(−0.4) + 2(0.6) = **0**
- This is why Mn²⁺ complexes are very pale — d–d transitions are spin-forbidden.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the neutral-atom d count (subtract the oxidation state first).
- Placing CN⁻ as weak field (it's among the strongest).
- Assigning low spin to tetrahedral complexes routinely.
- Forgetting that d¹–d³ and d⁸–d¹⁰ octahedral have no high/low choice.

activity.prompt: [Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is octahedral. What is its spin-only magnetic moment in BM? (Cr = Z 24)

quiz.q: In octahedral splitting, e_g orbitals are:
quiz.why: In octahedral splitting the e_g orbitals point toward the ligands, so they rise by +0.6Δo (and t₂g fall by 0.4Δo).
In the spectrochemical series CO is at the strong-field end, with Cl⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < CO.
A tetrahedral complex has only four ligands and none point directly at the orbitals, so Δt ≈ 4/9 Δo.
Fe²⁺ is d⁶. CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand, giving low spin t₂g⁶ with all electrons paired, so the complex is diamagnetic.

scenes.text: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; add a drop of water and it turns blue.
Water ligands split Cu²⁺'s d orbitals; it absorbs orange-red light and we see the complementary blue.

steps.title: Colour and Jahn–Teller
steps.body:
- Complexes absorb light to promote an electron t₂g → e_g (d–d transition); the observed colour is the **complementary** colour
- Δo = hc/λ_absorbed; in kJ/mol, Δo ≈ 119600/λ(nm)
- No d electrons (d⁰) or full d¹⁰ → no d–d colour (e.g. Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺ colourless)
- **Jahn–Teller**: unevenly filled e_g (d⁹ Cu²⁺, high-spin d⁴) distorts octahedra, usually elongating the z-axis

steps.title: Valence bond view
steps.body:
- [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻: Ni²⁺ d⁸, strong ligand pairs electrons → **dsp²**, square planar, diamagnetic
- [NiCl₄]²⁻: weak ligand → **sp³**, tetrahedral, 2 unpaired (2.83 BM)
- [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺: inner-orbital d²sp³, diamagnetic; [CoF₆]³⁻: outer-orbital sp³d², paramagnetic
- VBT cannot explain colour quantitatively — one reason CFT/LFT replaced it.

steps.title: Solved: Δo from colour
steps.body:
[Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs at about 498 nm and appears purple.

- Δo ≈ 119600/498 ≈ **240 kJ/mol**
- A stronger ligand would shift absorption to shorter wavelength.

steps.title: Complexes around us
steps.body:
- EDTA titration measures water hardness (Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺)
- Haemoglobin (Fe), chlorophyll (Mg), vitamin B₁₂ (Co)
- Cisplatin in cancer chemotherapy
- Extraction of gold and silver via cyanide complexes
- Wilkinson's catalyst [RhCl(PPh₃)₃] for hydrogenation

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a complex 'has the colour it absorbs'.
- Expecting Zn²⁺ complexes to be coloured.
- Mixing VBT inner/outer labels with high/low spin wrongly — inner orbital ↔ low spin.
- Forgetting Jahn–Teller applies to degenerate unequal occupation.

statements.s: [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is colourless.
[NiCl₄]²⁻ is square planar and diamagnetic.
Cu²⁺ octahedral complexes often show Jahn–Teller elongation.
Chlorophyll contains iron.

quiz.q: Observed colour of a complex is:
quiz.why: A complex absorbs some wavelengths of visible light, and what we see is the transmitted complementary colour, not the absorbed one.
Ni²⁺ is d⁸ and CN⁻ is a strong ligand that pairs electrons, giving a square planar dsp² complex.

quiz.q: Ion likely to show Jahn–Teller distortion:
quiz.why: Jahn–Teller distortion arises in uneven occupation of degenerate orbitals. Cu²⁺ (d⁹, e_g³) is strongly affected, while Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) and Cr³⁺ (d³) are symmetric.

quiz.q: EDTA titration is used to measure:
quiz.why: EDTA is a hexadentate chelating ligand that binds Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ strongly, so EDTA titration measures total water hardness.

quiz.q: Absorption at 600 nm corresponds to Δo of about:

questions.q: EDTA is a ___ ligand:
questions.why: EDTA has six donor atoms (two N and four carboxylate O), so it is hexadentate and wraps around the metal ion.

questions.q: Name ending for metal in an anionic complex:
questions.why: When the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate, e.g. ferrate or cuprate.

questions.q: Spin-only moment of 1 unpaired electron:
questions.why: μ = √(n(n+2)) = √3 = 1.73 BM for one unpaired electron.

questions.q: Oxidation state of Co in [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl:
questions.why: The complex ion is [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ because one Cl⁻ is outside. NH₃ is neutral and two Cl⁻ give −2, so x − 2 = +1 and Co = +3.

questions.q: Number of geometric isomers of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]:
questions.why: Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has just two geometric isomers: cis (like groups adjacent) and trans (opposite).

questions.q: Weak-field ligands generally give:
questions.why: Weak-field ligands give a small Δo, below the pairing energy P, so electrons occupy e_g orbitals before pairing, giving high-spin complexes.

questions.q: Assertion: Tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin. Reason: Δt is much smaller than Δo.
questions.why: Both statements are true: Δt ≈ 4/9 Δo is smaller than the pairing energy, so electrons stay unpaired (high spin). The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: CFSE of a low-spin d⁶ octahedral complex (ignoring pairing):
questions.why: Low-spin d⁶ is t₂g⁶ e_g⁰: CFSE = 6 × (−0.4Δo) = −2.4Δo.

questions.q: Total stereoisomers of [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺:
questions.why: trans-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ is achiral (1 form), while the cis form is chiral and exists as d and l enantiomers, so total = 3.

questions.q: Case: A Co(III) complex has μ = 0 BM. Likely ligand set:
questions.why: μ = 0 means all electrons are paired, so Co³⁺ (d⁶) is low spin. NH₃ is strong enough to give this, while H₂O and F⁻ are weak and give high spin.

questions.q: [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ spin-only moment:
questions.why: Fe³⁺ is d⁵ and H₂O is a weak-field ligand, so it is high spin with 5 unpaired electrons: μ = √35 = 5.92 BM.

questions.q: Which pair are coordination isomers?
questions.why: Coordination isomers swap ligands between the cationic and anionic complex ions, as in [Co(NH₃)₆][Cr(CN)₆] and [Cr(NH₃)₆][Co(CN)₆]. The others show geometric, ionisation or linkage isomerism.

questions.q: EAN of Ni in [Ni(CO)₄]:
questions.why: Effective atomic number = Z − oxidation state + 2 × coordination number: Ni(0) has 28 electrons and four CO donate 8, so EAN = 36 (krypton configuration).

questions.q: [CoCl₄]²⁻ (tetrahedral) is blue while [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is pink. The blue complex absorbs at ___ wavelength than the pink one:
questions.why: The tetrahedral complex has a smaller splitting (Δt) and a weaker field ligand, so it absorbs lower energy light, i.e. longer wavelength, and appears blue. The pink complex absorbs at shorter wavelength.

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons and hybridisation in [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻ (low spin):
questions.why: Mn³⁺ is d⁴. With strong-field CN⁻ it is low spin, t₂g⁴, giving 2 unpaired electrons, and the inner d²sp³ orbitals are used for bonding.

courses.title: B.Sc Chemistry · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page sheets for inorganic, organic and physical units, a timed solved practice set, and a 20-question mock exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall key rules and equations of each unit
Learners can solve mixed numericals under time pressure
Learners can avoid the most common exam slips

scenes.text: Sameer turns each unit into five rules and one exception, written on a single index card.
He reads them on the bus every day of exam week.

steps.title: Inorganic
steps.body:
- Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l; Cr, Cu exceptions
- Born–Haber: ΔH_f = ΔH_sub + IE + ½D + EA + U
- Fajans: small/high-charge cation + large anion → covalent
- VSEPR SN 2–6 → linear, trigonal, tetrahedral, TBP, octahedral; lone pairs equatorial in TBP
- MO: BO = (Nb − Na)/2; O₂ paramagnetic; s–p mixing for B₂–N₂
- CFT: t₂g −0.4Δo, e_g +0.6Δo; μ = √(n(n + 2))

steps.title: Organic
steps.body:
- Acidity ↑ with −I/−R stabilisation of conjugate base
- Carbocations 3° > 2° > 1°; carbanions reverse; rearrangement by 1,2-shifts
- CIP: atomic number; lowest priority away; R clockwise
- 2ⁿ stereoisomers minus meso duplicates
- SN2: 1°, inversion, aprotic; SN1: 3°, racemisation, protic; E2 anti-periplanar, Zaitsev (Hofmann with bulky base)

steps.title: Slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Removing 3d before 4s
- R/S reversal when H points toward you
- SN2 at 3° carbon
- CN⁻ as weak-field
- Counting double bonds as two VSEPR domains

quiz.why: PCl₅ has five bond pairs and no lone pairs on P, so its steric number is 5 and the shape is trigonal bipyramidal.
Alkyl radicals are stabilised by hyperconjugation with neighbouring C–H bonds, so tertiary is most stable and methyl and vinyl are the least.
Ni²⁺ is d⁸ and CN⁻ is strong-field, so [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is dsp² square planar with all electrons paired, hence diamagnetic.
A meso compound has stereocentres but an internal mirror plane, so the molecule as a whole is achiral and optically inactive.
Among alkali chlorides the cation sizes increase down the group, and lattice energy falls with size. Na⁺ is the smallest cation here, so NaCl has the highest lattice energy.

scenes.text: Ritu notices that 0.693, 0.0591, 2.303 and 96485 appear in almost every physical chemistry paper.
She learns where each comes from, so she never misplaces them.

steps.title: Thermodynamics & kinetics
steps.body:
- ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT; Kirchhoff ΔH₂ = ΔH₁ + ΔC_pΔT
- ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG° = −RT ln K = −nFE°
- First order: k = (2.303/t) log(a/(a − x)); t½ = 0.693/k
- Zero order t½ = a/2k; second order t½ = 1/ka
- log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)

steps.title: Electrochemistry & equilibria
steps.body:
- Λm = 1000κ/c; α = Λm/Λm°; Ka = cα²/(1 − α)
- E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q; log K = nE°/0.0591
- m = (M/nF) It; 1 F = 96485 C
- pH (weak acid) = ½(pKa − log c); Henderson pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA])
- Ksp: AB = s², AB₂ = 4s³, A₂B₃ = 108s⁵

activity.prompt: Match the constant to its meaning.

quiz.q: Ksp of Ca₃(PO₄)₂ in terms of s:
quiz.why: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ ⇌ 3Ca²⁺ + 2PO₄³⁻, so [Ca²⁺] = 3s and [PO₄³⁻] = 2s. Ksp = (3s)³(2s)² = 27 × 4 s⁵ = 108s⁵.
For zero order, [A] = a − kt. Half the reactant is gone when kt = a/2, so t½ = a/2k, which depends on initial amount.
ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96485 × 1.0 ≈ −193,000 J = −193 kJ. A positive E° always gives a negative ΔG°.
For a weak acid, [H⁺] = √(Ka·C) = √(10⁻⁵ × 0.1) = 10⁻³ M, so pH = ½(pKa − log C) = ½(5 + 1) = 3.
Al³⁺ needs 3 F of charge per mole of Al, so 3 F deposits exactly 1 mol = 27 g.

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved mixed set

scenes.text: Set a timer, attempt every question, then read the solutions.
Track which unit costs you the most marks and revisit that course.

steps.title: Paper technique
steps.body:
- Mechanisms: always show curly arrows, intermediates and stereochemistry
- Numericals: formula → substitution with units → answer
- Inorganic: draw the splitting diagram before counting electrons

steps.title: Solved: mixed 1
steps.body:
Predict shape and magnetism of [CoF₆]³⁻.

- Co³⁺ d⁶, F⁻ weak → t₂g⁴e_g², 4 unpaired → paramagnetic (4.90 BM)
- Octahedral, outer-orbital sp³d²

steps.title: Solved: mixed 3
steps.body:
pH after mixing 50 mL 0.1 M CH₃COOH and 25 mL 0.1 M NaOH (pKa 4.74)?

- Acid 5 mmol, base 2.5 mmol → 2.5 mmol HA + 2.5 mmol A⁻
- pH = pKa = **4.74** (half-equivalence point)

activity.prompt: Can you do these without notes?
items: Draw the MO diagram of O₂ and N₂
Derive the first-order integrated rate law
Write the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl
Assign R/S for a given Fischer projection
Name a complex with an anionic sphere
Calculate EMF with the Nernst equation

quiz.why: At half-equivalence half the weak acid is converted to its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa + log 1 = pKa.
XeF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs on Xe, so steric number 6. That means sp³d² hybridisation with a square planar shape.

quiz.q: tert-Butyl chloride in water mainly undergoes:
quiz.why: A tertiary halide forms a stable tertiary carbocation, and water is a polar protic solvent that stabilises ions, so the reaction goes by SN1. SN2 is blocked by steric hindrance.

quiz.q: Ea from k doubling between 300 and 310 K is about:
quiz.why: Using ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) with ratio 2: Ea = 8.314 × 0.693/(1.075 × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 54 kJ/mol. This is the standard 'rate doubles per 10 K' result.
Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹, so nine d electrons fill four orbitals with pairs and leave one orbital half-filled, giving 1 unpaired electron.
He₂⁺ has 3 electrons: σ1s² (bonding) and σ*1s¹ (antibonding). Bond order = (2 − 1)/2 = 0.5, so the ion exists but is weakly bound.

questions.q: Pauli's principle limits each orbital to:
questions.why: Pauli's exclusion principle allows at most 2 electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

questions.q: Which is a polar aprotic solvent?
questions.why: Acetone is polar but has no O–H or N–H bond, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds: it is polar aprotic. Water, ethanol and acetic acid are protic.

questions.q: Unit of molar conductivity:
questions.why: Molar conductivity Λm = κ/c, so its unit is S cm² mol⁻¹. S cm⁻¹ is the unit of conductivity.

questions.q: Which has zero dipole moment?
questions.why: CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so its two C=O bond dipoles cancel and the dipole moment is zero. SO₂, NH₃ and H₂O are bent or pyramidal, so dipoles do not cancel.

questions.q: Number of radial nodes in 4s:
questions.why: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 4 − 0 − 1 = 3 for a 4s orbital.

questions.q: Shape of SF₄:
questions.why: SF₄ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (steric number 5), giving a see-saw shape.

questions.q: Molecularity of an elementary bimolecular step:
questions.why: Molecularity is the number of species colliding in an elementary step. A bimolecular step involves two species, so molecularity is 2.

questions.q: pH of a buffer with [A⁻]/[HA] = 10 and pKa 4.74:
Assertion: O₂ is paramagnetic. Reason: It has two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals.
questions.why: Both are true: in molecular orbital theory O₂ has two unpaired electrons in separate π* orbitals, so it is paramagnetic. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: (R)-2-bromobutane + CH₃S⁻ (DMF) gives:
questions.why: Methylthiolate is a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF), so SN2 occurs with inversion: (R)-2-bromobutane gives the (S)-thioether, not a racemate.

questions.q: Ksp of BaSO₄ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. Solubility in water:
questions.why: BaSO₄ ⇌ Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ gives Ksp = s², so s = √(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 10⁻⁵ M.

questions.q: Spin-only μ of [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺:
questions.why: Ni²⁺ is d⁸. In the weak-field octahedral aqua complex it has two unpaired electrons in e_g, so μ = √(2 × 4) = 2.83 BM.

questions.q: Case: 3.0 A passes for 30 min through molten NaCl. Mass of Na (M = 23):
ΔH = −50 kJ, ΔS = −100 J/K. At 600 K the reaction is:
questions.why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −50 − 600 × (−0.100) = −50 + 60 = +10 kJ. A positive ΔG means non-spontaneous at 600 K.

questions.q: Most acidic hydrogen:
questions.why: The acidity of C–H rises with s-character of carbon: sp (50%) > sp² (33%) > sp³ (25%). The ethynyl carbanion is the most stable, so ethyne is the most acidic.

questions.q: Rate constants 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 300 K and 4.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 320 K. Ea:
For Cu²⁺ + Zn → Cu + Zn²⁺, at what [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] does E become zero (E° = 1.10 V)?
questions.why: E = E° − (0.0591/2) log Q. E = 0 gives log Q = 2 × 1.10/0.0591 ≈ 37, so Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] ≈ 10³⁷ (the cell has run to equilibrium).

questions.q: How many stereoisomers does CH₃CH(OH)CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ (pentane-2,3-diol) have?
questions.why: Pentane-2,3-diol has two stereocentres with different substituents, so there is no meso form. Stereoisomers = 2² = 4.

questions.q: Which complex shows both geometric and optical isomerism?
questions.why: [Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ has a cis form (chiral, a d/l pair) and a trans form, so it shows both geometric and optical isomerism. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [Ni(CO)₄] have just one form, and [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has no optical isomers.

uni-bsc-life.title: B.Sc Life Sciences — core papers, unit by unit
uni-bsc-life.description: Cell biology, genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry and ecology & evolution for B.Sc Life Sciences, Botany, Zoology and Biotechnology students, with solved problems and unit exams.

courses.title: Cell Biology · structure, membranes, organelles, division
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Cell theory and prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells, membrane structure and transport including water potential, the endomembrane system and energy organelles, and the cell cycle with mitosis and meiosis.
outcomes: Learners can compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and do magnification calculations
Learners can explain membrane transport and solve water-potential problems
Learners can trace the secretory pathway and describe organelle functions
Learners can track chromosome number and DNA content through the cell cycle

lessons.title: Cell theory, cell types and microscopy

scenes.text: In the first practical, Rhea sees onion peel cells as neat bricks under a light microscope.
Her teacher asks: the image is 5 mm across at ×1000 — how big is the real cell?

steps.title: Cell theory and two cell plans
steps.body:
**Cell theory** (Schleiden and Schwann, 1838–39; Virchow, 1855): all organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

- **Prokaryotes** (bacteria, archaea): no nucleus (nucleoid), no membrane-bound organelles, 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S), usually circular DNA, often plasmids, cell wall of peptidoglycan in bacteria
- **Eukaryotes**: nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes (60S + 40S), linear chromosomes with histones

steps.title: Solved: magnification
steps.body:
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.

- Image 5 mm at ×1000 ⇒ 5 mm/1000 = 0.005 mm = **5 μm**
- A 2 μm bacterium imaged at ×40,000 by an electron microscope appears 80 mm wide.

Resolution: light microscope ≈ 0.2 μm; electron microscope ≈ 0.2 nm or better.

steps.title: Solved: why cells are small
steps.body:
Compare cubes of side 1 μm and 2 μm.

- 1 μm: surface area 6 μm², volume 1 μm³ ⇒ SA : V = **6**
- 2 μm: 24 μm², 8 μm³ ⇒ SA : V = **3**
- Doubling the side halves SA : V, so exchange with the surroundings becomes too slow for large cells.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 70S + 80S = 150S thinking (Svedberg units are not additive: 50S + 30S = 70S).
- Confusing magnification with resolution.
- Unit slips: 1 mm = 1000 μm; 1 μm = 1000 nm.
- Saying prokaryotes have no DNA outside the nucleoid (plasmids exist).

activity.prompt: Prokaryote, eukaryote or both?

quiz.q: 'Omnis cellula e cellula' is associated with:
quiz.why: 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (all cells from cells) was stated by Rudolf Virchow, who added that new cells come only from pre-existing cells. Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of 50S and 30S subunits. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S).

quiz.q: An image 12 mm wide at ×400. Actual size:
quiz.why: Actual size = image size/magnification = 12 mm/400 = 0.03 mm = 30 μm.

quiz.q: As a cell grows larger, SA : V:
quiz.why: As a cell grows, volume rises faster (as r³) than surface area (as r²). So SA : V falls, making exchange with the surroundings harder.

quiz.q: Resolution limit of a light microscope is about:
quiz.why: A light microscope's resolution is limited by the wavelength of visible light, about 0.2 μm (200 nm). Electron microscopes resolve much finer detail.

scenes.text: Spinach sprinkled with salt goes limp; dipped in plain water it crisps up again.
Water moves from higher to lower water potential across membranes — osmosis.

steps.title: Fluid mosaic model
steps.body:
Proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972): a phospholipid bilayer with embedded and peripheral proteins that can move laterally; cholesterol modulates fluidity in animal cells; glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer face act in recognition.

Transport:
- **Simple diffusion**: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂), down the gradient
- **Facilitated diffusion**: via channels/carriers, no ATP (glucose via GLUT, water via aquaporins)
- **Active transport**: against the gradient using ATP; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP
- **Bulk transport**: endocytosis (phago-, pino-, receptor-mediated) and exocytosis

steps.title: Water potential
steps.body: ψ = ψs + ψp (MPa). Pure water at atmospheric pressure has ψ = 0; solutes make ψs negative; turgor makes ψp positive. Water moves from **higher (less negative) to lower (more negative)** ψ.

steps.title: Solved: direction of water flow
steps.body:
A cell has ψs = −0.8 MPa and ψp = +0.3 MPa; it is placed in a solution of ψ = −0.7 MPa.

- ψ(cell) = −0.8 + 0.3 = −0.5 MPa
- −0.5 > −0.7 ⇒ water moves **out of the cell** into the solution
- Prolonged loss leads to plasmolysis.

steps.title: Solved: tonicity
steps.body:
- Red blood cells in distilled water (hypotonic) swell and may burst (haemolysis)
- In 0.9% saline (isotonic) they keep shape — why IV drips use normal saline
- Plant cells in hypertonic solution plasmolyse; the wall prevents bursting in hypotonic solution

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying water moves toward 'higher' water potential.
- Calling facilitated diffusion active because proteins are involved.
- Forgetting ψp can be negative (tension in xylem).
- Mixing up hypotonic and hypertonic with respect to which solution.

activity.prompt: A plant cell has ψs = −1.2 MPa and ψp = +0.5 MPa. What is its water potential in MPa?

quiz.q: The fluid mosaic model was proposed by:
quiz.why: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972, with proteins floating in a fluid lipid bilayer. Danielli and Robertson proposed earlier sandwich models.
Per ATP, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. The net charge movement makes it electrogenic.
