Aquaporins are protein channels that let water cross the membrane by facilitated diffusion, down its potential gradient and without energy. They are not for glucose.

quiz.q: ψ of pure water at atmospheric pressure:
quiz.why: Water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure is defined as zero. Solutes lower it to negative values.
In a hypertonic solution water leaves the red blood cell by osmosis, so the cell shrinks and becomes crenated. Bursting happens in hypotonic solutions.

scenes.text: A pancreatic β-cell makes insulin and ships it out. Where is it built, packed and dispatched?
Ribosomes on rough ER → Golgi → secretory vesicles → plasma membrane: a factory line inside the cell.

steps.title: Organelle roles
steps.body:
- **Nucleus**: double envelope with pores; nucleolus makes rRNA/ribosome subunits
- **Rough ER**: ribosome-studded; makes secretory and membrane proteins
- **Smooth ER**: lipid synthesis, detoxification, Ca²⁺ storage (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle)
- **Golgi**: modifies (glycosylation), sorts and packages; cis face receives, trans face ships
- **Lysosomes**: acid hydrolases at pH ≈ 5; autophagy
- **Mitochondria**: double membrane, cristae, own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes — evidence for **endosymbiosis**; site of Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
- **Chloroplasts**: thylakoids (light reactions), stroma (Calvin cycle); also own DNA
- **Cytoskeleton**: microtubules (≈ 25 nm, tubulin), intermediate filaments (≈ 10 nm), microfilaments (≈ 7 nm, actin)

steps.title: Solved: pulse–chase reasoning
steps.body:
Cells are given radioactive amino acids for 3 minutes (pulse), then unlabelled ones (chase). Label appears in sequence:

- 3 min: rough ER
- ~20 min: Golgi
- ~120 min: secretory vesicles near the membrane

Conclusion: secretory proteins travel **RER → Golgi → vesicles → exterior**.

steps.title: Solved: matching cells to organelles
steps.body:
- Liver cell detoxifying drugs → abundant smooth ER
- Plasma cell secreting antibodies → abundant rough ER and Golgi
- Sperm tail / flight muscle → many mitochondria
- White blood cell digesting bacteria → many lysosomes

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles (they are not membrane-bound).
- Placing protein synthesis in the Golgi (Golgi modifies; ribosomes synthesise).
- Forgetting mitochondria have their own DNA but still import most proteins encoded by nuclear genes.
- Confusing cis and trans Golgi faces.

activity.prompt: Order the path of a secretory protein.
items: mRNA translated by ribosome on rough ER
Polypeptide enters ER lumen and folds
Transport vesicle carries it to the cis Golgi
Modified and sorted through to the trans Golgi
Secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane (exocytosis)

quiz.q: Lysosomal enzymes work best at pH:
quiz.why: Lysosomal acid hydrolases work best in the acidic lumen at about pH 5, which is maintained by proton pumps. They are far less active at the cytosol's pH.

quiz.q: Evidence for endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria:
quiz.why: Mitochondria have circular DNA and 70S ribosomes like bacteria, which supports the endosymbiotic theory that they came from engulfed bacteria.

quiz.q: Main role of smooth ER in liver:
quiz.why: Smooth ER in liver cells carries enzymes that detoxify drugs and poisons and make lipids and steroids. Protein secretion is a job of rough ER.
Microfilaments are thin actin polymers, about 7 nm wide. Microtubules are tubulin and intermediate filaments are keratin and similar proteins.
The nucleolus transcribes rRNA genes and assembles ribosomal subunits, so it is the 'ribosome factory'.

scenes.text: A single fertilised egg becomes a baby with trillions of cells — by mitosis.
Each parent's gametes are made by meiosis, which shuffles chromosomes so siblings differ.

steps.title: Phases and checkpoints
steps.body:
- **Interphase**: G₁ (growth), S (DNA replication), G₂ (preparation); G₀ for non-dividing cells
- Checkpoints at G₁/S, G₂/M and the spindle (metaphase) checkpoint, controlled by cyclins and CDKs
- **Mitosis**: prophase, metaphase (chromosomes at the plate), anaphase (sister chromatids separate), telophase; then cytokinesis (cleavage furrow in animals, cell plate in plants)
- **Meiosis I** (reductional): prophase I — leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata visible), diakinesis; homologues separate in anaphase I
- **Meiosis II** (equational): sister chromatids separate

steps.title: Solved: DNA content (C) and chromosome number
steps.body:
For a diploid cell with 2C DNA in G₁:

- After S: **4C**, still 2n chromosomes (each with two chromatids)
- After mitosis: each daughter 2C, 2n
- After meiosis I: 2C, **n** chromosomes
- After meiosis II: **C**, n

Human G₂ cell: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids.

steps.title: Solved: genetic variation
steps.body:
An organism with 2n = 8 has 4 homologous pairs.

- Independent assortment alone gives 2⁴ = **16** chromosome combinations in gametes
- Humans (n = 23): 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million — before crossing over adds more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking chromosome number doubles in S phase (DNA doubles; chromosome count stays).
- Placing crossing over in prophase II.
- Calling meiosis II reductional.
- Confusing chromatids with chromosomes when counting.

activity.prompt: Order the substages of prophase I.
items: Leptotene — chromosomes condense
Zygotene — homologues pair (synapsis)
Pachytene — crossing over
Diplotene — chiasmata visible as homologues separate
Diakinesis — terminalisation, envelope breaks down

quiz.why: DNA is replicated in the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle. G₁ and G₂ are growth gaps and M is division.
Crossing over happens in pachytene of prophase I, when homologous chromosomes are paired and recombination nodules mediate the exchange.
In anaphase I the homologous chromosomes separate and go to opposite poles, which halves the chromosome number (reductional division). Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.

quiz.q: A cell with 4C DNA and 2n chromosomes is in:
quiz.why: 4C DNA with 2n chromosomes means DNA has replicated but the cell has not divided, which is G₂ (after S, before M).
Plant cells have a rigid cell wall, so they divide the cytoplasm by building a cell plate. Animal cells pinch in by a cleavage furrow.

questions.q: Powerhouse of the cell:
questions.why: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP by aerobic respiration, so they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

questions.q: Which lacks a nucleus?
questions.why: A bacterium is a prokaryote and has no membrane-bound nucleus. Amoeba, yeast and plant cells are eukaryotes with a nucleus.

questions.q: Movement of water across a membrane down its potential gradient:
questions.why: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane down its water potential gradient, with no energy needed.

questions.q: Number of chromatids in a human cell at metaphase of mitosis:
questions.why: At metaphase of mitosis the DNA is already replicated, so each of the 46 chromosomes has two sister chromatids: 46 × 2 = 92.

questions.q: Cell organelle that sorts and packages proteins:
questions.why: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or other destinations, like a post office.

questions.q: The checkpoint that ensures all chromosomes attach to the spindle:
questions.why: The metaphase (spindle assembly) checkpoint delays anaphase until every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, which prevents aneuploidy.

questions.q: Assertion: Mitochondria have 70S ribosomes. Reason: Mitochondria are thought to descend from engulfed bacteria.
questions.why: Both are true: mitochondria have 70S ribosomes like bacteria, and this fits the idea that they descend from engulfed bacteria. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Cell: ψs = −0.6 MPa, ψp = 0.2 MPa. Solution: ψ = −0.2 MPa. Water moves:
questions.why: Cell ψ = ψs + ψp = −0.6 + 0.2 = −0.4 MPa. Water moves from higher (less negative, −0.2) to lower (−0.4) potential, so it moves into the cell.

questions.q: 2n = 12. Number of chromosome combinations from independent assortment:
questions.why: With n = 6 pairs, each pair assorts independently into either gamete, so the combinations number 2ⁿ = 2⁶ = 64.

questions.q: Case: A drug blocks microtubule assembly. Cells will arrest at:
questions.why: Without microtubules no spindle can form, so chromosomes cannot align. The spindle checkpoint holds cells in metaphase/mitosis.

questions.q: If a G₁ cell has 10 pg DNA, a cell at the end of meiosis I has:
questions.why: A G₁ cell is 2C = 10 pg. After S it is 4C = 20 pg. Meiosis I separates homologues into two cells, each 2C = 10 pg.

questions.q: Ouabain inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Immediate effect:
questions.why: Ouabain blocks the pump that expels 3 Na⁺ per cycle, so Na⁺ leaks in and cannot be removed, and intracellular Na⁺ rises first. K⁺ inside then falls rather than rises.

questions.q: Which observation best distinguishes meiosis I from mitosis?
questions.why: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes, occurs only in prophase I of meiosis. Envelope breakdown, spindle formation and condensation also occur in mitosis.

questions.q: I-cell disease: lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of delivered to lysosomes. The defect lies in:
questions.why: In I-cell disease the Golgi fails to add the mannose-6-phosphate tag to lysosomal enzymes, so they are not sorted to lysosomes and are secreted instead.

questions.q: A spherical cell doubles its radius. Its SA : V ratio:
questions.why: For a sphere SA : V = 4πr²/(4/3 πr³) = 3/r. Doubling r halves the ratio.

courses.title: Genetics · Mendel to populations
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Mendelian crosses with probability and chi-square, extensions such as codominance, multiple alleles and epistasis, linkage mapping, and sex-linked inheritance with Hardy–Weinberg population genetics.
outcomes: Learners can predict monohybrid and dihybrid ratios and test them by chi-square
Learners can recognise modified ratios from gene interaction
Learners can compute recombination frequencies and map distances
Learners can analyse pedigrees and apply Hardy–Weinberg

scenes.text: In the 1860s Gregor Mendel counted thousands of pea plants and found tidy ratios like 3 : 1.
Modern students test whether their own counts fit such ratios using the chi-square test.

steps.title: Laws and ratios
steps.body:
- **Segregation**: allele pairs separate into gametes
- **Independent assortment**: genes on different chromosomes assort independently
- Monohybrid F₂: 3 : 1 phenotype, 1 : 2 : 1 genotype
- Dihybrid F₂: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
- Test cross (with homozygous recessive): 1 : 1 or 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 reveals a heterozygote
- Probability: multiply for independent events; for AaBbCc × AaBbCc, P(aabbcc) = (1/4)³ = 1/64

steps.title: Solved: branch probability
steps.body:
AaBb × Aabb. Probability of A_bb offspring?

- P(A_) from Aa × Aa = 3/4
- P(bb) from Bb × bb = 1/2
- P = 3/4 × 1/2 = **3/8**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using percentages instead of counts in chi-square.
- Wrong degrees of freedom (classes − 1).
- Adding probabilities that should be multiplied.
- Assuming independent assortment for linked genes.

activity.prompt: In AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd, what fraction of offspring are aabbccdd? Enter as a decimal (4 d.p.).

quiz.why: In an F₂ monohybrid cross the genotypes appear as 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. The 3 : 1 ratio is the phenotypic ratio.

quiz.q: A test cross involves crossing with:
quiz.why: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive parent. Since it gives only recessive alleles, offspring phenotypes reveal the unknown parent's genotype.

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom for a 3 : 1 chi-square test:
quiz.why: Degrees of freedom = number of classes − 1. A 3 : 1 ratio has 2 classes, so df = 1.
For AaBb × AaBb, P(AA) = 1/4 and P(BB) = 1/4 independently, so P(AABB) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

quiz.q: A χ² value below the critical value means:
quiz.why: A χ² below the critical value means the deviation from expected could be due to chance, so the data fit the expected ratio and we do not reject the hypothesis.

scenes.text: A child has blood group O while the parents are A and B. The family is worried.
If both parents are heterozygous (IAi × IBi), an O child is perfectly expected — 1 in 4.

steps.title: Beyond simple dominance
steps.body:
- **Incomplete dominance**: heterozygote intermediate (snapdragon red × white → pink; F₂ 1 : 2 : 1)
- **Codominance**: both expressed (IAIB → AB blood group)
- **Multiple alleles**: ABO has IA, IB, i (IA = IB > i)
- **Lethal alleles**: yellow coat in mice, Yy × Yy → 2 : 1 (YY dies)
- **Epistasis** (one gene masks another), dihybrid F₂ modifications:
  - Recessive epistasis 9 : 3 : 4 (coat colour in mice/Labradors)
  - Dominant epistasis 12 : 3 : 1 (fruit colour in summer squash)
  - Complementary genes 9 : 7 (sweet pea flower colour)
  - Duplicate genes 15 : 1

steps.title: Solved: ABO cross
steps.body:
IAi × IBi:

- Gametes IA, i × IB, i
- Offspring IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B), ii (O) — each **1/4**
- So an A × B couple can have children of all four blood groups.

steps.title: Solved: identifying a ratio
steps.body:
F₂ of two white-flowered pea lines gives 180 purple : 140 white.

- Total 320; 180/320 = 9/16, 140/320 = 7/16
- Ratio **9 : 7** ⇒ complementary gene action: both dominant alleles (C_P_) needed for purple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the AB blood group 'incomplete dominance'.
- Forgetting lethal genotypes reduce the total (2 : 1, not 3 : 1).
- Confusing epistasis (between genes) with dominance (between alleles of one gene).
- Not reducing raw counts to sixteenths before naming a ratio.

activity.prompt: Match the F₂ ratio to the gene interaction.

quiz.why: In AB blood both IA and IB alleles are expressed, so both A and B antigens are present. This is codominance.

quiz.q: Parents A (IAi) and O can have children:
quiz.why: Parents IAi × ii give gametes IA or i from one and only i from the other, so children are IAi (A) or ii (O).
A 9 : 7 ratio is a modified dihybrid ratio from complementary genes, where both dominant alleles are needed for the trait and anything else gives the same phenotype.

quiz.q: Yellow × yellow mice give 2 yellow : 1 non-yellow because:
quiz.why: Yellow × yellow giving 2 : 1 means yellow is dominant and the YY homozygote dies before birth. Only Yy (yellow) and yy survive.

quiz.q: Snapdragon pink × pink gives red : pink : white:
quiz.why: Pink snapdragons are heterozygous (incomplete dominance), so pink × pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

lessons.title: Linkage, crossing over and gene mapping

scenes.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit flies did not give 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in test crosses for some gene pairs.
His student Sturtevant used the recombinant percentages to draw the first genetic map (1913).

steps.title: Recombination and maps
steps.body:
- Linked genes lie on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together
- **Recombination frequency (RF)** = recombinants/total × 100; 1% RF = 1 map unit (centimorgan, cM)
- RF is at most ~50% (indistinguishable from independent assortment)
- **Three-point cross**: parental classes are most frequent, double crossovers (DCO) least; the gene that 'switches' in DCO relative to parentals is in the middle
- Coefficient of coincidence (CoC) = observed DCO/expected DCO; **interference = 1 − CoC**

steps.title: Solved: two-point map
steps.body:
Test cross AaBb (coupling AB/ab) × aabb: AB 420, ab 380, Ab 105, aB 95.

- Recombinants = 105 + 95 = 200 of 1000
- RF = **20%** ⇒ genes are **20 cM** apart

steps.title: Solved: interference
steps.body:
Genes A–B 10 cM, B–C 20 cM. In 1000 progeny, 10 double crossovers were observed.

- Expected DCO = 0.10 × 0.20 × 1000 = 20
- CoC = 10/20 = 0.5
- Interference = **0.5** (one crossover halves the chance of a nearby second)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting parentals as recombinants when the parent was in repulsion (Ab/aB).
- Adding distances without accounting for double crossovers in long intervals.
- Expecting RF above 50%.
- Forgetting that DCO classes determine the middle gene.

activity.prompt: A test cross gives 460 + 440 parental and 52 + 48 recombinant offspring. Map distance in cM?

quiz.why: One map unit (1 centimorgan) is defined as 1% recombination frequency between two genes.
The recombination frequency cannot exceed 50%, since unlinked genes give 50% recombinants by independent assortment.

quiz.q: Least frequent class in a three-point cross:
quiz.why: A double crossover needs two crossover events in the same region, which is rare, so it is the least frequent class.
Interference I = 1 − coefficient of coincidence = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

quiz.q: The first genetic map was made by:
quiz.why: Alfred Sturtevant, a student of T. H. Morgan, made the first genetic map in 1913 using Drosophila X-linked genes.

scenes.text: A grandfather is red–green colour-blind; his daughters see normally, but one grandson is colour-blind.
X-linked recessive traits skip to grandsons through carrier daughters.

steps.title: Sex-linked inheritance and pedigrees
steps.body:
- **X-linked recessive** (colour blindness, haemophilia): more males affected; affected father → all daughters carriers, no sons affected through him
- **X-linked dominant**: affected father → all daughters affected
- **Autosomal recessive**: can skip generations; unaffected parents can have affected children
- **Autosomal dominant**: every affected person usually has an affected parent; both sexes equally
- **Y-linked**: father to all sons

steps.title: Hardy–Weinberg
steps.body: For alleles A (p) and a (q), p + q = 1 and genotype frequencies are **p² + 2pq + q² = 1** if: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no selection. Deviation signals evolution.

steps.title: Solved: carrier frequency
steps.body:
An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 2500 births.

- q² = 1/2500 ⇒ q = 0.02, p = 0.98
- Carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.98 × 0.02 = **0.0392 ≈ 1 in 25**
- Most recessive alleles hide in healthy carriers.

steps.title: Solved: X-linked cross
steps.body:
Carrier mother (XᴮXᵇ) × normal father (XᴮY):

- Daughters: ½ XᴮXᴮ, ½ XᴮXᵇ (carriers) — none affected
- Sons: ½ XᴮY normal, ½ XᵇY **affected**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking q = frequency of affected individuals (that is q²).
- Applying H–W to small, inbred or selected populations.
- Thinking X-linked recessive traits pass father → son.
- Calling every 'skipped generation' trait X-linked (autosomal recessive also skips).

activity.prompt: In a population, 16% show a recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of heterozygotes (as a decimal)?

quiz.why: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disease, so it affects males much more and passes through carrier females.

quiz.q: Affected father, X-linked dominant trait: daughters are:
quiz.why: A father passes his only X to every daughter, so for an X-linked dominant trait all his daughters are affected. Sons get his Y.
With q = 0.1, p = 0.9, so AA = p² = 0.81.
Hardy–Weinberg needs no selection, no mutation, random mating and a large population. Natural selection changes allele frequencies, so it violates equilibrium.

quiz.q: A trait passed from father to all sons only:
quiz.why: A Y-linked trait goes from father to all sons only, because only sons inherit the Y chromosome.

questions.q: Phenotypic ratio of F₂ dihybrid cross:
questions.why: With independent assortment, an F₂ dihybrid cross gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.q: Genes close together on one chromosome are:
questions.why: Genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together and are called linked.

questions.q: Unit of map distance:
questions.why: Genetic map distance is measured in centimorgans (cM), named after T. H. Morgan.

questions.q: Possible blood groups of children of AB × O parents:
questions.why: IAIB × ii gives children IAi (group A) or IBi (group B). Neither AB nor O is possible.

questions.q: Test cross ratio for a dihybrid heterozygote (unlinked):
questions.why: A heterozygous dihybrid (AaBb) test-crossed with aabb produces four equal gamete types, giving a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.q: In H–W equilibrium with p = 0.7, 2pq =
questions.why: With p = 0.7, q = 0.3, and heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42.

questions.q: Assertion: Two unaffected parents can have a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. Reason: Both may be heterozygous carriers.
questions.why: Both true: two heterozygous carriers (Aa × Aa) are unaffected, but each child has a 1/4 chance of aa. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: F₂ counts 92 white : 23 yellow : 7 green in squash suggest:
questions.why: The total is 122 and 12:3:1 would predict 91.5 : 22.9 : 7.6, close to 92 : 23 : 7. A 9 : 3 : 4 or 9 : 7 split would not fit.

questions.q: P(aaB_) from AaBb × AaBb:
Case: Genes A and B show 8% recombination, B and C 3%, A and C 11%. Gene order:
questions.why: A–C (11) equals A–B + B–C (8 + 3), the largest distance being the sum of the others, so B lies between A and C: A–B–C.

questions.q: A colour-blind man marries a carrier woman. Probability their son is colour-blind:
questions.why: The mother is a carrier (XᴮXᵇ), and a son gets his X from her and Y from the father. So half the sons receive Xᵇ and are colour-blind: 1/2.

questions.q: χ² = 9.2 with df = 3 (critical 7.815 at p = 0.05). Conclusion:
questions.why: χ² = 9.2 exceeds the critical value 7.815 at df = 3 and p = 0.05, so the deviation is unlikely to be chance and the hypothesised ratio is rejected.

questions.q: A recessive allele has frequency 0.01. Among affected children, what fraction come from carrier × carrier matings (random mating)?
questions.why: Affected children (aa) come mostly from Aa × Aa matings: carriers (2pq ≈ 0.02) are far more common than affected parents (q² = 0.0001), so nearly all affected children have carrier parents.

questions.q: Expected DCO for 1000 progeny, intervals 12 cM and 15 cM, interference 0.4:
questions.why: Expected DCO if independent = 0.12 × 0.15 × 1000 = 18. Coincidence = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6, so observed = 18 × 0.6 = 10.8.

questions.q: Recessive epistasis in Labradors: BbEe × BbEe gives black : brown : yellow =
questions.why: In recessive epistasis, ee masks the B/b gene: E_B_ is black (9/16), E_bb brown (3/16), and ee gives yellow (3 + 1 = 4/16): 9 : 3 : 4.

courses.title: Molecular Biology · DNA to protein to regulation
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: DNA structure and Chargaff's rules, semi-conservative replication and its enzymes, transcription and RNA processing, and translation, the genetic code and the lac operon.
outcomes: Learners can apply Chargaff's rules and DNA dimensions
Learners can interpret the Meselson–Stahl experiment and replication enzymes
Learners can transcribe and process genes
Learners can translate mRNA and predict lac operon behaviour

scenes.text: Laid end to end, the DNA in one human cell would stretch about two metres — yet it fits in a nucleus a few micrometres wide.
The double helix and its packing make that possible.

steps.title: The double helix (B-DNA)
steps.body:
Proposed by Watson and Crick (1953), using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

- Two antiparallel strands (5′→3′ and 3′→5′), right-handed
- Sugar–phosphate backbone outside; bases inside
- About 10 bp per turn (≈ 10.5 in solution), pitch ≈ 3.4 nm, rise 0.34 nm per bp, diameter ≈ 2 nm
- **Chargaff's rules**: A = T, G = C; A–T 2 hydrogen bonds, G–C 3
- Packaging: DNA wraps histone octamers (~146–147 bp per nucleosome) → 30 nm fibre → loops → chromosome

steps.title: Solved: base composition
steps.body:
A DNA sample has 30% adenine.

- T = 30%; G + C = 40% ⇒ **G = C = 20%**
- Higher G–C content means higher melting temperature (3 H-bonds and stronger stacking).

steps.title: Solved: length of DNA
steps.body:
Human haploid genome ≈ 3 × 10⁹ bp.

- Length = 3 × 10⁹ × 0.34 nm = 1.02 × 10⁹ nm ≈ **1 m**
- A diploid cell has ≈ **2 m**
- A 1000 bp fragment makes about 100 turns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying A pairs with G (purine–purine pairs don't fit).
- Applying Chargaff's rules to single-stranded genomes.
- Writing strands parallel.
- Confusing nucleoside (base + sugar) with nucleotide (+ phosphate).

activity.prompt: A double-stranded DNA has 18% cytosine. What percentage is adenine?

quiz.q: Hydrogen bonds in a G–C pair:
quiz.why: A G–C base pair is joined by three hydrogen bonds, whereas A–T has two.

quiz.q: Distance between adjacent base pairs in B-DNA:
quiz.why: In B-DNA adjacent base pairs are stacked 0.34 nm apart, and one helix turn of 10 bp is 3.4 nm.
The two DNA strands run in opposite directions (5′→3′ and 3′→5′), so they are antiparallel.
Chargaff found that in double-stranded DNA A equals T and G equals C, which reflects complementary base pairing.
G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and stronger stacking than A–T, so DNA with more G–C needs more heat to melt and has a higher Tm.

scenes.text: In 1958, Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria on heavy ¹⁵N, switched them to ¹⁴N, and spun their DNA in a caesium chloride gradient.
After one generation every DNA molecule was 'half-heavy' — proof that replication is semi-conservative.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body:
- **Semi-conservative**: each daughter duplex has one old and one new strand
- Origin(s) of replication; bidirectional forks (bacteria: one origin; eukaryotes: many)
- **Helicase** unwinds; **SSB proteins** hold strands apart; **topoisomerase/gyrase** relieves supercoiling
- **Primase** lays an RNA primer; **DNA polymerase III** (bacteria) extends 5′→3′ only
- **Leading strand** continuous; **lagging strand** in Okazaki fragments
- **DNA polymerase I** removes primers and fills gaps; **ligase** seals nicks
- Proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease keeps error rates very low

steps.title: Solved: Meselson–Stahl generations
steps.body:
Start: all ¹⁵N/¹⁵N (heavy). Grow in ¹⁴N.

- Generation 1: 100% hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N)
- Generation 2: 50% hybrid, 50% light
- Generation 3: 25% hybrid, 75% light
- Conservative replication would have given heavy + light bands at generation 1 — not seen.

steps.title: Solved: replication time
steps.body:
An E. coli chromosome of 4.6 × 10⁶ bp replicates bidirectionally from one origin with each fork moving ≈ 1000 nt/s.

- Each fork copies 2.3 × 10⁶ bp
- Time ≈ 2.3 × 10⁶/1000 = 2300 s ≈ **38 minutes**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DNA polymerase can start a new strand without a primer.
- Synthesising 3′→5′.
- Assigning Okazaki fragments to the leading strand.
- Forgetting that ligase, not polymerase, makes the final phosphodiester bond between fragments.

activity.prompt: Match the enzyme to its job.

quiz.why: In generation 2 of the Meselson–Stahl experiment, half the DNA is hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) and half is light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N), which supports semi-conservative replication.
Okazaki fragments are short pieces made on the lagging strand, which is synthesised discontinuously, away from the fork.
DNA polymerases add nucleotides only to a free 3′-OH, so synthesis runs 5′→3′.
DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds.

quiz.q: Primers in DNA replication are made of:
quiz.why: Primase builds the short RNA primers that give DNA polymerase a free 3′-OH to start from.

scenes.text: A master cookbook stays in the library (nucleus); cooks get photocopies of single recipes.
In eukaryotes the copy is edited — capped, tailed and spliced — before leaving.

steps.title: Making RNA
steps.body:
- RNA polymerase reads the **template (antisense) strand** 3′→5′ and builds RNA 5′→3′; RNA has the same sequence as the **coding strand** (U for T)
- Bacteria: one RNA polymerase (core α₂ββ′ω + σ factor); σ recognises promoter boxes near −10 (TATAAT) and −35 (TTGACA)
- Termination: rho-independent (GC-rich hairpin + U-tract) or rho-dependent
- Eukaryotes: RNA Pol I (most rRNA), Pol II (mRNA), Pol III (tRNA, 5S rRNA); TATA box ≈ −25 to −30
- **Processing** of pre-mRNA: 5′ cap (7-methylguanosine), 3′ poly(A) tail, **splicing** of introns by the spliceosome; alternative splicing makes multiple proteins from one gene

steps.title: Solved: template to mRNA
steps.body:
Template strand: 3′-TACGGATTC-5′.

- mRNA (complementary, 5′→3′): **5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′**
- Coding strand: 5′-ATGCCTAAG-3′ (same as mRNA with T)

steps.title: Solved: splicing arithmetic
steps.body:
A gene has exons of 150, 200 and 250 nt and two introns of 1000 nt each.

- Primary transcript ≈ 2600 nt (exons + introns)
- Mature mRNA coding region ≈ 600 nt (plus cap and tail)
- If all exons are coding, the protein ≈ 600/3 − 1 = **199 amino acids** (last codon a stop).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing mRNA complementary to the coding strand.
- Forgetting U replaces T.
- Thinking prokaryotic mRNA is spliced and capped like eukaryotic mRNA.
- Mixing which RNA polymerase makes mRNA in eukaryotes (Pol II).

activity.prompt: Complete the facts.
activity.text: In eukaryotes, mRNA is made by RNA polymerase ___, introns are removed by the ___, and a poly(A) tail is added at the ___ end.

quiz.why: The σ factor lets bacterial RNA polymerase recognise and bind promoters, which gives initiation its specificity. It does not splice or cap RNA.
mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so its sequence matches the coding strand with U replacing T.

quiz.q: tRNA in eukaryotes is made by:
quiz.why: In eukaryotes RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA genes, 5S rRNA and some small RNAs. Pol II makes mRNA and Pol I makes most rRNA.
Removing introns and joining exons is splicing, carried out by the spliceosome. Capping and tailing add to the ends of the RNA.
The Pribnow box, centred about 10 bases before the transcription start, has consensus TATAAT. TTGACA is the −35 element.

lessons.title: Translation, the genetic code and the lac operon

scenes.text: E. coli in your gut makes lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce.
Jacob and Monod explained this switch with the lac operon (Nobel Prize, 1965).

steps.title: The code and translation
steps.body:
- Triplet, non-overlapping, commaless, nearly universal, **degenerate** (61 sense codons for 20 amino acids)
- Start **AUG** (Met; fMet in bacteria); stops **UAA, UAG, UGA**
- **Wobble**: flexible pairing at the codon's third base
- Ribosome sites: **A** (aminoacyl), **P** (peptidyl), **E** (exit); peptidyl transferase activity lies in rRNA (a ribozyme)
- Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge each tRNA with the correct amino acid

steps.title: The lac operon
steps.body:
Genes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase) share promoter and operator.

- **Negative control**: LacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) inactivates the repressor → transcription
- **Positive control**: when glucose is low, cAMP rises; CAP–cAMP binds near the promoter and boosts transcription
- High expression needs **lactose present AND glucose low**

steps.title: Solved: translating mRNA
steps.body:
5′-AUG GCU UAC UGG UGA-3′

- AUG Met, GCU Ala, UAC Tyr, UGG Trp, UGA stop
- Peptide: **Met–Ala–Tyr–Trp** (4 amino acids)
- A point mutation UAC → UAA would give a premature stop (nonsense mutation).

steps.title: Solved: lac scenarios
steps.body:
- Glucose high, lactose absent → repressor bound → **off**
- Glucose high, lactose present → repressor off but little CAP–cAMP → **low**
- Glucose low, lactose present → **high**
- lacI⁻ mutant (no repressor) → **constitutive** expression

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking lactose itself binds the repressor (the inducer is allolactose).
- Saying high glucose raises cAMP (it lowers it).
- Counting the stop codon as an amino acid.
- Calling the code 'ambiguous' — it is degenerate (many codons → one amino acid), not ambiguous.

a.text: An E. coli culture has lactose but no glucose. What happens at the lac operon?

choices.label: Repressor inactivated and CAP–cAMP bound: high expression

a2.text: Remember the inducer. Try again: lactose present, glucose absent.

b.text: Now glucose is added while lactose remains. Expression becomes…

choices.label: Low — cAMP falls so CAP no longer activates

b2.text: Glucose lowers cAMP levels. Choose again.

end.text: The lac operon needs both a signal that lactose is present and a signal that glucose is scarce.

quiz.why: There are three stop codons, UAA, UAG and UGA, and they code for no amino acid.
AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine. UAG and UGA are stop codons.
Allolactose, an isomer of lactose, binds the LacI repressor and lifts repression, so it induces the lac operon.

quiz.q: The peptide bond is formed by:
quiz.why: The peptide bond is made by the ribosomal RNA of the large subunit (peptidyl transferase), so the ribosome acts as a ribozyme.

options: one codon codes many amino acids
many codons code one amino acid
quiz.why: Degeneracy (redundancy) means several different codons can code for the same amino acid. It does not mean one codon codes for many.

questions.q: Sugar in DNA:
questions.why: DNA contains deoxyribose, which lacks the 2′-OH of ribose. RNA contains ribose.

questions.q: Base absent from DNA:
questions.why: DNA has A, T, G and C, whereas uracil replaces thymine in RNA. So uracil is absent from DNA.

questions.q: Codons per amino acid for methionine:
questions.why: Methionine is coded by only AUG, which is also the start codon, so it has a single codon.

questions.q: Enzyme that unwinds DNA:
questions.why: Helicase unwinds the DNA double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between the bases, using ATP.

questions.q: Eukaryotic mRNA 5′ end carries:
questions.why: Eukaryotic mRNA gets a 7-methylguanosine cap at its 5′ end, and a poly(A) tail at the 3′ end.

questions.q: If 20% of bases are G in dsDNA, A is:
questions.why: G = C = 20%, so G + C = 40%. The rest 60% is A + T, split equally, so A = 30%.

questions.q: Assertion: The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously. Reason: DNA polymerase works only 5′→3′.
questions.why: Both true: DNA polymerase works only 5′→3′, so on the strand running the other way it has to make short fragments discontinuously. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Template 3′-TACAAACCG-5′ encodes:
questions.why: The template 3′-TAC AAA CCG-5′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG UUU GGC-3′. These code for Met, Phe and Gly.

questions.q: Meselson–Stahl generation 3 in ¹⁴N gives hybrid DNA fraction:
questions.why: After 3 generations there are 8 molecules, of which 2 are hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) and 6 are light, so the hybrid fraction is 2/8 = 1/4.

questions.q: Case: A lacI⁻ mutant grows in glucose-free medium without lactose. lacZ expression:
questions.why: With no LacI repressor the operon cannot be repressed, and with no glucose CAP–cAMP is active, so lacZ is expressed at a high level even without lactose.

questions.q: A frameshift (single-base insertion) near the start of a gene usually:
questions.why: Adding one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is read differently, usually giving a wrong, truncated protein.

questions.q: An mRNA of 1500 coding nucleotides (including stop) encodes a protein of:
questions.why: 1500 nucleotides = 500 codons. One is the stop codon, which has no amino acid, so the protein has 499 amino acids.

questions.q: A bacterium has a 5 × 10⁶ bp genome, one origin, forks at 500 nt/s. Replication time:
questions.why: With one origin, two forks each copy half the genome: 2.5 × 10⁶ bp per fork at 500 nt/s = 5000 s ≈ 83 min.

questions.q: A mutation in the lac operator so the repressor can't bind (Oᶜ) causes:
options: constitutive expression of the cis operon
questions.why: An operator-constitutive (Oᶜ) mutation stops the repressor binding, so the operon next to it on the same DNA is expressed all the time. It acts in cis only.

questions.q: Why do UV-induced thymine dimers block replication?
options: They distort the helix so polymerase stalls
questions.why: UV links adjacent thymines covalently, which distorts the helix, so replication polymerase stalls at the dimer. The dimer does not add phosphates, break sugars or change T to U.

courses.title: Biochemistry · biomolecules, enzymes, metabolism
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, enzyme kinetics and inhibition, cellular respiration with ATP accounting, and photosynthesis including the Calvin cycle and C₄/CAM adaptations.
outcomes: Learners can identify glycosidic linkages and protein structure levels
Learners can use the Michaelis–Menten equation and identify inhibition types
Learners can account for ATP yield from glucose
Learners can explain light reactions, the Calvin cycle and C₄ plants

scenes.text: A cow lives on grass; we cannot. Both starch and cellulose are chains of glucose.
The difference is the bond: α(1→4) in starch versus β(1→4) in cellulose.

steps.title: Key structures
steps.body:
**Carbohydrates**
- Maltose: glucose α(1→4) glucose; lactose: galactose β(1→4) glucose; sucrose: glucose α(1→2)β fructose (non-reducing)
- Starch: amylose α(1→4), amylopectin + α(1→6) branches; glycogen more branched; cellulose β(1→4)

**Proteins**
- 20 standard amino acids joined by peptide bonds (condensation)
- Primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix ~3.6 residues/turn, β-sheet; H-bonds), tertiary (3-D fold), quaternary (subunits, e.g. haemoglobin α₂β₂)

**Lipids**
- Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids, ester bonds); saturated vs unsaturated (cis double bonds kink chains)
- Phospholipids amphipathic → bilayers; steroids (cholesterol)

steps.title: Solved: counting
steps.body:
- A pentapeptide forms with **4** water molecules released (n − 1 peptide bonds)
- Number of different tripeptides possible from 20 amino acids: 20³ = **8000**
- A triglyceride's formation releases **3** water molecules.

steps.title: Solved: reducing sugars
steps.body: Benedict's test is positive for glucose, maltose, lactose (free anomeric carbon) but **negative for sucrose**, since both anomeric carbons are tied up in the α(1→2)β bond. Boiling sucrose with dilute acid hydrolyses it, then the test turns positive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling sucrose a reducing sugar.
- Thinking denaturation breaks peptide bonds (it disrupts higher-order structure).
- Saying unsaturated fats are solid at room temperature (usually liquid oils).
- Confusing amylopectin (some branches) with glycogen (heavily branched).

activity.prompt: Match the molecule with its linkage.

quiz.why: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar because its glucose and fructose are linked through both anomeric carbons, leaving no free aldehyde or ketone. Maltose, lactose and cellobiose are reducing.
An α-helix is a secondary structure, held by hydrogen bonds along the polypeptide backbone.

quiz.q: Haemoglobin shows quaternary structure because it has:
quiz.why: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide subunits (α₂β₂), and the arrangement of several subunits is quaternary structure.

quiz.q: Bond linking glycerol to fatty acids:
quiz.why: Fatty acids are linked to glycerol by ester bonds, formed by condensation of an OH and a COOH.

quiz.q: Water molecules released when forming a decapeptide:
quiz.why: Each peptide bond releases one water, and n amino acids form n − 1 bonds. A decapeptide (10) therefore releases 9 water molecules.

scenes.text: A supermarket with 5 tills serves faster as more customers arrive — until all tills are busy.
Enzymes saturate the same way: velocity approaches Vmax as substrate rises.

steps.title: Kinetics
steps.body:
- **Michaelis–Menten**: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km = [S] at which v = Vmax/2 (lower Km ≈ higher apparent affinity)
- **Lineweaver–Burk**: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km
- kcat = Vmax/[E]ₜ (turnover number); kcat/Km = catalytic efficiency
- Inhibition: **competitive** (Km↑, Vmax unchanged; overcome by more substrate), **non-competitive** (Vmax↓, Km unchanged), **uncompetitive** (both ↓)
- Enzyme classes (EC): oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases, and translocases (added in 2018)

steps.title: Solved: using the equation
steps.body:
Km = 2 mM, Vmax = 100 μmol/min.

- [S] = 2 mM: v = 100 × 2/4 = **50**
- [S] = 6 mM: v = 100 × 6/8 = **75**
- [S] = 18 mM (9 Km): v = 90 — reaching 90% Vmax needs [S] = 9Km

steps.title: Solved: diagnosing inhibition
steps.body:
With an inhibitor, apparent Km rises from 2 to 6 mM but Vmax stays 100.

- Pattern ⇒ **competitive**
- Example in medicine: methotrexate competes with folate for dihydrofolate reductase; ethanol is used against methanol poisoning by competing for alcohol dehydrogenase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Km a rate (it is a concentration).
- Reading the x-intercept of a Lineweaver–Burk plot as +1/Km (it is −1/Km).
- Saying competitive inhibitors lower Vmax.
- Assuming optimum temperature is always 37 °C (it varies by organism).

activity.prompt: An enzyme has Km = 4 mM and Vmax = 200 units. What is v at [S] = 12 mM?

quiz.why: Km is defined as the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax.
A competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site, so more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax. This raises the apparent Km while Vmax stays the same.
In the Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v against 1/[S]) the y-intercept, where 1/[S] = 0, equals 1/Vmax.
An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex, which lowers both Vmax and apparent Km.

quiz.q: Enzymes that hydrolyse bonds with water belong to class:
quiz.why: Hydrolases catalyse the breaking of bonds by adding water. They are class EC 3.

scenes.text: A 100 m sprinter relies mostly on anaerobic pathways; a marathoner on aerobic respiration.
Glycolysis alone gives 2 ATP per glucose; with oxygen, about 30–32.

steps.title: Stages (per glucose)
steps.body:
- **Glycolysis** (cytosol): glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP, 2 NADH
- **Link reaction** (matrix): 2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl-CoA + 2 CO₂ + 2 NADH
- **Krebs cycle** (matrix, two turns): 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP (or GTP), 4 CO₂
- **Electron transport chain + chemiosmosis** (inner membrane): O₂ is the final electron acceptor; ATP synthase uses the proton gradient (Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory)
- Anaerobic: pyruvate → lactate (muscle) or ethanol + CO₂ (yeast), regenerating NAD⁺; only 2 ATP

steps.title: Solved: modern ATP count
steps.body:
Using P/O ratios ≈ 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂:

- Substrate-level: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (Krebs) = 4
- NADH: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 × 2.5 = 25
- FADH₂: 2 × 1.5 = 3
- Total ≈ **32 ATP** (≈ 30 if glycolytic NADH enters via the glycerol-phosphate shuttle). Older textbooks quote 36–38 using whole-number P/O ratios of 3 and 2.

steps.title: Solved: CO₂ bookkeeping
steps.body: Six carbons of glucose leave as CO₂: 2 in the link reaction + 4 in the Krebs cycle = **6 CO₂**. Water is produced at Complex IV when O₂ accepts electrons.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose.
- Placing glycolysis in mitochondria.
- Saying oxygen is needed for glycolysis.
- Quoting 38 ATP as the only correct answer — state the P/O assumptions.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of aerobic respiration of glucose.
items: Glycolysis in the cytosol
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion
Oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl-CoA
Krebs cycle in the matrix
Electron transport chain and ATP synthase on the inner membrane

quiz.why: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses 2 in the preparatory phase, so the net gain is 2 ATP per glucose.

quiz.q: Final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration:
quiz.why: In aerobic respiration oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the transport chain and is reduced to water.

quiz.q: CO₂ released per glucose in the Krebs cycle (two turns):
quiz.why: Each turn of the Krebs cycle releases 2 CO₂, and one glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA, so 2 turns release 4 CO₂. The other 2 CO₂ come from pyruvate oxidation.
Peter Mitchell proposed the chemiosmotic theory: a proton gradient drives ATP synthesis.
Yeast converts pyruvate to acetaldehyde and then ethanol with release of CO₂. Lactate is made in animal muscle.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis: light reactions, Calvin cycle, C₄ and CAM

scenes.text: In a hot Maharashtra summer, sugarcane keeps growing fast while wheat would struggle.
Sugarcane is a C₄ plant: it concentrates CO₂ around RuBisCO and avoids photorespiration.

steps.title: Light reactions (thylakoids)
steps.body:
- **PS II** (P680) splits water: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂ (O₂ comes from water)
- Electrons flow PS II → plastoquinone → cytochrome b₆f → plastocyanin → **PS I** (P700) → ferredoxin → NADP⁺ reductase (the Z-scheme)
- Proton gradient drives ATP synthase (photophosphorylation)
- Non-cyclic flow gives ATP + NADPH + O₂; cyclic flow (PS I only) gives ATP only

steps.title: Calvin cycle (stroma)
steps.body:
- **Carboxylation**: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ onto RuBP (5C) → 2 × 3-PGA
- **Reduction**: 3-PGA → G3P using ATP and NADPH
- **Regeneration** of RuBP using ATP
- Per CO₂: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; per glucose (6 CO₂): **18 ATP + 12 NADPH**
- **C₄** (maize, sugarcane): PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into oxaloacetate in mesophyll; Kranz anatomy; CO₂ released in bundle sheath ⇒ little photorespiration
- **CAM** (pineapple, cacti): stomata open at night, CO₂ stored as malate; temporal separation

steps.title: Solved: oxygen origin
steps.body: If plants are given H₂¹⁸O and normal CO₂, the released O₂ is labelled; with C¹⁸O₂ and normal water, it is not. Conclusion: **photosynthetic O₂ comes from water** (shown with isotope experiments by Ruben and Kamen).

steps.title: Solved: Calvin cycle arithmetic
steps.body:
To make one G3P (3C), the cycle fixes 3 CO₂.

- ATP: 3 × 3 = **9**
- NADPH: 3 × 2 = **6**
- Two G3P make one glucose ⇒ 18 ATP, 12 NADPH

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying O₂ comes from CO₂.
- Calling the Calvin cycle 'dark reactions' that happen only at night (they need light-made ATP/NADPH and run by day).
- Assigning PEP carboxylase to the bundle sheath (it is in the mesophyll).
- Confusing CAM (temporal) with C₄ (spatial) separation.

activity.prompt: Where does each process occur?

quiz.q: Primary CO₂ acceptor in C₃ plants:
quiz.why: In C₃ plants the first CO₂ acceptor is RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate), fixed by RuBisCO to give 3-PGA.

quiz.q: First stable product in C₄ plants:
quiz.why: In C₄ plants PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells to oxaloacetate, a 4-carbon acid, hence 'C₄'.
Photosystem I has the reaction-centre chlorophyll P700, named for peak absorption at 700 nm. P680 is photosystem II.

quiz.q: ATP per glucose in the Calvin cycle:
quiz.why: The Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP per CO₂ fixed, so 6 CO₂ for one glucose needs 6 × 3 = 18 ATP.
CAM plants open stomata at night to take in CO₂ when it is cooler, saving water, and store it as malic acid for the day.

questions.q: Monomer of starch:
questions.why: Starch is a polymer of α-glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: Site of glycolysis:
questions.why: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol (cytoplasm), and needs no organelle.

questions.q: Enzyme that fixes CO₂ in C₃ plants:
questions.why: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle of C₃ plants. PEP carboxylase is the C₄ enzyme.

questions.q: Proteins are polymers of:
questions.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.q: Non-competitive inhibitors:
questions.why: Non-competitive inhibitors bind a site other than the active site, lowering Vmax; excess substrate cannot overcome them.

questions.q: Source of O₂ in photosynthesis:
questions.why: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water (photolysis), not from CO₂.

questions.q: Assertion: C₄ plants show little photorespiration. Reason: CO₂ is concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells.
questions.why: Both true: C₄ plants concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells, which suppresses RuBisCO's oxygenase activity and so photorespiration. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: v at [S] = Km/3 as a fraction of Vmax:
NADH produced per glucose in the Krebs cycle:
questions.why: The Krebs cycle makes 3 NADH per turn, and one glucose gives 2 turns, so 6 NADH.

questions.q: Case: A poison blocks Complex IV. Immediate effects:
options: O₂ consumption stops and ATP yield falls sharply
questions.why: Blocking Complex IV stops electrons reaching O₂, so oxygen use stops and the proton gradient cannot be maintained, causing ATP yield to fall sharply. Glycolysis continues for a while.

questions.q: Lineweaver–Burk: y-intercept 0.02 min/μmol, x-intercept −0.5 mM⁻¹. Km and Vmax:
questions.why: y-intercept 1/Vmax = 0.02, so Vmax = 50 μmol/min. x-intercept −1/Km = −0.5, so Km = 2 mM.

questions.q: Total ATP per glucose with P/O 2.5 (NADH) and 1.5 (FADH₂), malate–aspartate shuttle:
questions.why: 2 ATP (glycolysis) + 2 ATP (Krebs, substrate-level) = 4; 10 NADH × 2.5 = 25; 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 3. Total = 4 + 25 + 3 = 32.

questions.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle produce one glucose?
questions.why: Each turn fixes one CO₂. A 6-carbon glucose needs six CO₂, so 6 turns.

questions.q: Ethanol treatment for methanol poisoning works because ethanol is a ___ inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase for methanol:
questions.why: Ethanol competes with methanol for the same active site of alcohol dehydrogenase, so less toxic formaldehyde forms. That is competitive inhibition.

questions.q: Uncouplers like 2,4-dinitrophenol make mitochondria:
options: consume O₂ but make less ATP, releasing heat
questions.why: Uncouplers let protons leak back across the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase. O₂ use continues but less ATP is made, and the energy is lost as heat.

courses.title: Ecology & Evolution · energy, populations, communities, change
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Energy flow and ecological pyramids, population growth models and estimation, species interactions and succession, and evolution by natural selection, drift and speciation.
outcomes: Learners can calculate productivity and energy transfer
Learners can use exponential and logistic models and mark–recapture
Learners can classify interactions and stages of succession
Learners can explain selection types, drift and speciation with examples

scenes.text: A reserve may hold millions of grass plants, thousands of deer, but only a handful of tigers.
Most energy is lost at each step up the food chain — roughly 90% each time.

steps.title: Productivity and transfer
steps.body:
- **GPP** (gross primary productivity): total photosynthetic capture; **NPP = GPP − R** (plant respiration)
- **Ten per cent law** (Lindeman, 1942): about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level
- Pyramid of **energy** is always upright; **biomass** can be inverted (open-ocean phytoplankton vs zooplankton); **numbers** can be inverted (one tree, many insects)
- Detritus food chains recycle nutrients; decomposers are essential

steps.title: Solved: energy along a chain
steps.body:
Producers fix 10,000 J.

- Primary consumers ≈ 1000 J
- Secondary ≈ 100 J
- Tertiary ≈ **10 J** — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels.

steps.title: Solved: NPP
steps.body:
GPP = 2000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, plant respiration = 800.

- NPP = **1200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹** — the energy available to herbivores and decomposers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the pyramid of energy can be inverted.
- Treating the 10% figure as exact (it varies widely, ~5–20%).
- Forgetting decomposers in energy flow.
- Confusing biomass (standing crop) with productivity (rate).

activity.prompt: If producers fix 50,000 kJ, how much energy (kJ) reaches the secondary consumers by the 10% law?

quiz.why: Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity minus energy used in plant respiration: NPP = GPP − R.
The pyramid of energy is always upright, since energy is lost at each trophic level. Numbers and biomass pyramids can be inverted.
Raymond Lindeman proposed the 10% law in 1942: about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.

quiz.q: Inverted pyramid of biomass is seen in:
quiz.why: In the open ocean tiny phytoplankton reproduce fast but have a small standing biomass, so the biomass pyramid is inverted.

quiz.q: Organisms that recycle nutrients from dead matter:
quiz.why: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

story.title: Counting fish without draining the lake

scenes.text: A fisheries team tags 50 fish and releases them. A week later they catch 40 and find 10 tagged.
Proportion tagged in the sample ≈ proportion in the lake: about 200 fish.

steps.title: Growth models
steps.body:
- **Exponential**: dN/dt = rN ⇒ N = N₀e^(rt); doubling time ≈ 0.693/r
- **Logistic**: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K); S-shaped curve; growth fastest at N = K/2 (K = carrying capacity)
- r-selected (many offspring, little care) vs K-selected (few offspring, much care)
- Survivorship curves: Type I (humans), Type II (many birds), Type III (oysters, many plants)
- **Lincoln–Petersen index**: N = (M × C)/R

steps.title: Solved: logistic growth
steps.body:
r = 0.1 yr⁻¹, K = 1000, N = 500.

- dN/dt = 0.1 × 500 × (1 − 0.5) = **25 per year** (the maximum for this population)
- At N = 900: 0.1 × 900 × 0.1 = 9 per year

steps.title: Solved: mark–recapture
steps.body:
M = 50 marked, C = 40 caught, R = 10 recaptured.

- N = 50 × 40/10 = **200**
- Assumptions: marks not lost, marked animals mix randomly, closed population.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking logistic growth is fastest near K.
- Using percentage r directly in e^(rt) (convert 5% to 0.05).
- Ignoring mark–recapture assumptions (trap-shy animals bias estimates).
- Swapping Type I and Type III survivorship.

activity.label: Population size as a fraction of K

bands.text: Small population: growth nearly exponential but absolute numbers low.
Near K/2: the fastest absolute growth (maximum sustainable yield region).

quiz.q: Logistic growth rate is maximum at:
quiz.why: Logistic growth dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) is maximum when N = K/2, the point of the steepest growth.
Lincoln–Petersen: N = (marked first × second catch)/marked recaptured = 30 × 60/12 = 150.
Humans show type I survivorship: most individuals survive to old age and deaths cluster at the end.
Doubling time = ln 2/r = 0.693/0.07 ≈ 10 years.

quiz.q: K in the logistic model is:
quiz.why: K is the carrying capacity, the maximum population size the environment can sustain.

scenes.text: After a lava flow cools, nothing lives on it. Within years, lichens appear.
Over centuries, mosses, grasses, shrubs and finally forest follow — primary succession.

steps.title: Interactions
steps.body:
- Mutualism (+, +): lichens (alga + fungus), mycorrhizae
- Commensalism (+, 0): orchid on a mango tree (epiphyte)
- Parasitism (+, −): Cuscuta on host plants; tapeworms
- Predation (+, −): tiger and deer
- Competition (−, −): **Gause's principle** — two species with identical niches can't coexist indefinitely
- Amensalism (−, 0): Penicillium inhibiting bacteria
- **Keystone species** have disproportionate effects (e.g. sea otters controlling sea urchins and protecting kelp)

steps.title: Succession and biodiversity
steps.body:
- **Primary** succession: bare substrate (rock, lava); pioneers = lichens
- **Secondary**: after disturbance where soil remains (abandoned farm, burnt forest); faster
- Ends in a relatively stable **climax community**
- India includes parts of four global biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands)

steps.title: Solved: classify the interaction
steps.body:
- Cattle egret eating insects disturbed by grazing cattle → **commensalism**
- Clownfish and sea anemone → **mutualism** (protection and food scraps)
- Two barnacle species on the same rock, one excluding the other → **competition**

steps.title: Solved: order of a hydrosere
steps.body: Succession in a pond (hydrarch): phytoplankton → submerged plants → floating plants → reed-swamp → sedge meadow → woodland → forest climax. Water body gradually fills and becomes land.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling parasitism 'predation' or vice versa without noting that parasites usually don't kill quickly.
- Thinking succession always ends in forest (climate decides the climax).
- Confusing primary and secondary succession.
- Assuming keystone species are the most abundant ones.

activity.prompt: Match the example with the interaction.

quiz.q: Pioneers of primary succession on rock:
quiz.why: Lichens can grow on bare rock and begin soil formation, so they are the pioneers of primary succession on rock.
Commensalism is a (+, 0) interaction: one species benefits and the other is unaffected.
Gause's principle (competitive exclusion) says two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely.
Secondary succession starts where soil already exists, such as an abandoned field, so it is faster than primary succession.

quiz.q: A hotspot including India's southwest coast:
quiz.why: The Western Ghats and Sri Lanka form a biodiversity hotspot along India's southwest coast. Madagascar, the Caucasus and Sundaland are elsewhere.

scenes.text: During the Industrial Revolution soot darkened tree trunks, and dark peppered moths became common.
After clean-air laws, pale moths recovered — directional selection in both directions.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- **Natural selection** (Darwin and Wallace, 1858; Origin of Species 1859): variation, heritability, over-production, differential survival and reproduction
- Selection types: **stabilising** (human birth weight), **directional** (industrial melanism, antibiotic resistance), **disruptive** (two extremes favoured)
- **Genetic drift**: random change, strongest in small populations; founder effect, bottleneck (e.g. cheetahs' low diversity)
- Gene flow, mutation and non-random mating also change allele frequencies
- **Speciation**: allopatric (geographic isolation), sympatric (e.g. polyploidy in plants); reproductive isolation is key

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body:
- Fossils and transitional forms (e.g. Archaeopteryx)
- **Homologous** organs: same origin, different function (forelimbs of whale, bat, human) → divergent evolution
- **Analogous** organs: different origin, same function (wings of insects and birds) → convergent evolution
- Molecular similarities (DNA, protein sequences), vestigial organs, biogeography

steps.title: Solved: name the selection
steps.body:
- Bacteria treated with an antibiotic: resistant forms rise → **directional**
- Babies of very low and very high birth weight have higher mortality → **stabilising**
- Finches on an island where only very small and very large seeds exist → **disruptive**

steps.title: Solved: drift vs selection
steps.body: An island population of 20 lizards loses a neutral colour allele after a storm kills half at random. That is **genetic drift (bottleneck)**, not selection, because survival was unrelated to the allele.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying individuals evolve (populations do).
- Thinking organisms develop traits because they 'need' them (Lamarckian thinking).
- Calling bat and insect wings homologous.
- Assuming drift is important only in large populations (it matters most in small ones).

activity.prompt: Put these milestones in order.

events.text: Lamarck publishes his theory of inheritance of acquired characters
Darwin and Wallace present natural selection
On the Origin of Species published
Hardy and Weinberg describe genetic equilibrium

quiz.q: Antibiotic resistance spread is an example of:
quiz.why: Antibiotic resistance spreads because the resistant extreme is favoured under drug exposure, which is directional selection.

quiz.q: Wings of a bat and an insect are:
quiz.why: Bat and insect wings do the same job but evolved independently with different structure, so they are analogous. Homologous organs share an origin.

quiz.q: Founder effect is a type of:
quiz.why: The founder effect is genetic drift: a few founders carry a random sample of the original population's alleles.
Allopatric speciation needs geographic isolation, which stops gene flow so the populations diverge.
Evolution acts on populations, since it is a change in allele frequencies over generations. Individuals do not evolve in this sense.

questions.q: Producers in an ecosystem are:
questions.why: Producers make food by photosynthesis, so green plants are the producers. Fungi are decomposers.

questions.q: Organs with common origin but different function:
questions.why: Homologous organs share a common origin but may have different functions, as with a human arm and a whale flipper. Analogous organs share function but not origin.

questions.q: Carrying capacity is denoted:
questions.why: In the logistic model, K stands for carrying capacity. r is the growth rate and N the population size.

questions.q: Clownfish–sea anemone relationship:
questions.why: The clownfish is protected by the anemone and the anemone is cleaned and defended by the fish, so both benefit: mutualism.

questions.q: Pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem is often:
questions.why: A single tree supports many herbivorous insects, so the base is smaller than the next level and the pyramid of numbers is inverted.

questions.q: Genetic drift is strongest in:
questions.why: Genetic drift is random sampling error in allele frequencies, which is large in small populations and small in large ones.

questions.q: Assertion: The pyramid of energy is never inverted. Reason: Energy is lost as heat at every trophic transfer.
questions.why: Both true: energy is lost as heat at each transfer (second law of thermodynamics), so less is available at higher levels and the energy pyramid is never inverted.

questions.q: Mark 80, recapture sample 100 with 20 marked. Population:
questions.why: N = (marked × sample)/recaptured marked = 80 × 100/20 = 400.

questions.q: Succession on an abandoned farm is:
questions.why: An abandoned farm still has soil, so the succession there is secondary, not primary.

questions.q: Case: GPP = 30,000 kJ, R = 12,000 kJ, herbivores assimilate 10% of NPP. Energy to herbivores:
questions.why: NPP = GPP − R = 30,000 − 12,000 = 18,000 kJ. Herbivores assimilate 10%, so 0.1 × 18,000 = 1800 kJ.

questions.q: Sickle-cell heterozygotes have malaria resistance, keeping both alleles in the population. This is:
questions.why: Sickle-cell heterozygotes resist malaria, so both alleles are kept in the population. This is balancing selection by heterozygote advantage, not drift or directional selection.

questions.q: A population of 10⁴ grows exponentially at r = 0.0693 per year. Size after 30 years:
questions.why: Doubling time = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 years, so 30 years is 3 doublings: 10⁴ × 2³ = 8 × 10⁴.

questions.q: Wheat (hexaploid) arose partly through hybridisation and polyploidy. This illustrates:
questions.why: Polyploidy gives instant reproductive isolation without geographic separation, which is a type of sympatric speciation, as in wheat.

questions.q: Removing a keystone predator from a rocky shore most likely causes:
options: drop in diversity as a dominant competitor takes over
questions.why: A keystone predator (like the starfish Pisaster) keeps dominant competitors in check. Remove it and the dominant species (e.g. mussels) takes over, so diversity falls.

courses.title: B.Sc Life Sciences · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Key facts and formulas from every unit, a solved mixed set of problems and a 20-question mock exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall core facts and numbers
Learners can solve genetics and kinetics numericals
Learners can answer assertion–reason and case questions

scenes.text: Pooja makes one card per unit with the five facts examiners love.
She quizzes her roommate every night.

steps.title: Cells & genetics
steps.body:
- 70S (50S + 30S) vs 80S (60S + 40S); SA : V falls with size
- ψ = ψs + ψp; water to more negative ψ
- Na⁺/K⁺ pump 3 out, 2 in
- G₁ 2C → S → G₂ 4C; meiosis I reductional; crossing over in pachytene
- Ratios: 3 : 1, 1 : 2 : 1, 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, 9 : 3 : 4, 12 : 3 : 1, 9 : 7, 15 : 1, 2 : 1
- RF% = cM; interference = 1 − CoC; p² + 2pq + q² = 1

steps.title: Molecular biology
steps.body:
- B-DNA: 0.34 nm/bp, ~10 bp/turn, 2 nm wide; A = T, G = C
- Semi-conservative (Meselson–Stahl); 5′→3′; Okazaki on lagging
- σ factor, −10 TATAAT, −35 TTGACA; Pol II makes mRNA
- AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop
- lac operon high only with lactose present and glucose low

steps.title: Exam traps
steps.body:
- q vs q² in Hardy–Weinberg
- Template vs coding strand
- Chromosome vs chromatid counts
- 'Dark reactions' are not night-only

quiz.why: Heterozygotes = 2pq. With q = 0.3, p = 0.7, so 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42.
mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template: template 3′-GCA-5′ gives 5′-CGU-3′, with U in place of T.

quiz.q: Chromatids in a human G₂ nucleus:
quiz.why: In G₂ the DNA is already replicated, so each of the 46 chromosomes has two chromatids: 46 × 2 = 92.
A 9 : 7 ratio comes from complementary gene action, where both dominant alleles are needed for the trait.
Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, made of a 60S large and a 40S small subunit. (Svedberg units do not add arithmetically.)

scenes.text: 32 ATP, 18 ATP + 12 NADPH, 10%, K/2 — Tarun lists the numbers that show up in every paper.
Then he writes how each is derived, so he can rebuild them if he forgets.

steps.title: Biochemistry
steps.body:
- v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); competitive ↑Km; non-competitive ↓Vmax; uncompetitive both ↓
- Glycolysis net 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link 2 NADH; Krebs 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP; total ≈ 30–32 ATP
- Calvin: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂; 18 + 12 per glucose
- O₂ from water; PS II P680, PS I P700; C₄ = PEP carboxylase + Kranz; CAM = night stomata

steps.title: Ecology & evolution
steps.body:
- NPP = GPP − R; ≈ 10% transfer
- dN/dt = rN; rN(1 − N/K); max at K/2; N = MC/R
- Interactions: (+,+), (+,0), (+,−), (−,−), (−,0)
- Selection: stabilising, directional, disruptive; drift strongest in small populations

steps.title: Answering case questions
steps.body: Underline the data in the case, name the concept it tests, then calculate. Write units at every step.

activity.prompt: Match the number to its meaning.

quiz.q: NADPH per glucose in the Calvin cycle:
quiz.why: The Calvin cycle uses 2 NADPH per CO₂, so 6 CO₂ (one glucose) needs 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH.

quiz.q: Bottleneck effect is a form of:
quiz.why: A bottleneck cuts a population to a few random survivors, so allele frequencies change by chance. This is genetic drift.

quiz.q: PEP carboxylase is located in C₄ plant:
quiz.why: PEP carboxylase does the first CO₂ fixation in the mesophyll cells of C₄ plants. RuBisCO works in the bundle sheath.

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved mixed set

scenes.text: Give yourself 25 minutes for this set.
Mark yourself and revisit the course behind each mistake.

steps.title: Solved: genetics
steps.body:
A woman with blood group A whose father was O marries a man with group B whose mother was O. Probability their child is O?

- Woman IAi, man IBi
- P(ii) = ½ × ½ = **1/4**

steps.title: Solved: kinetics
steps.body:
An enzyme reaches 80% of Vmax at what [S] relative to Km?

- 0.8 = [S]/(Km + [S]) ⇒ 0.8Km = 0.2[S] ⇒ **[S] = 4Km**

steps.title: Solved: ecology
steps.body:
A population of 1200 has K = 2000 and r = 0.5. dN/dt?

- 0.5 × 1200 × (1 − 0.6) = **240 per unit time**

steps.title: Long-answer structure
steps.body: Definition → labelled diagram (described clearly) → mechanism/steps → example → significance. Examiners reward structure.

activity.prompt: Before the exam, can you:
items: Draw and label the fluid mosaic model
Draw a replication fork with all enzymes
Explain the lac operon in all four glucose/lactose conditions
Write the ATP balance sheet for glucose
Solve a three-point mapping problem
Explain the Z-scheme of photosynthesis

quiz.q: A × B parents (both heterozygous) — P(child AB):
quiz.why: For a child to be AB, the A-group parent (IAi) must pass IA (1/2) and the B-group parent (IBi) must pass IB (1/2): 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

quiz.q: Most frequent class in a test cross of linked genes:
quiz.why: In a test cross of linked genes the parental combinations stay together most of the time, so the parental classes are the most frequent. Recombinants are fewer.

quiz.q: Pyramid of biomass in the open ocean is often:
quiz.why: In the open ocean the standing biomass of fast-turnover phytoplankton is small compared with consumers, so the pyramid of biomass is inverted.

quiz.q: Which is NOT made by RNA Pol III?
quiz.why: RNA polymerase II makes mRNA. Pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA and some small RNAs.

quiz.q: Number of ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation per glucose (aerobic):
quiz.why: Substrate-level phosphorylation gives 2 ATP in glycolysis and 2 ATP (as GTP/ATP) in the Krebs cycle: 4 ATP. The rest comes from the electron transport chain.

questions.q: Cell theory states cells arise from:
questions.why: Cell theory, as completed by Virchow, says new cells arise only from pre-existing cells, not from non-living matter.

questions.q: DNA replication is:
questions.why: The Meselson–Stahl experiment showed that DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new DNA has one old and one new strand.

questions.q: Final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration:
questions.why: Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain and is reduced to water.

questions.q: Commensalism is:
questions.why: Commensalism is (+, 0): one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

questions.q: Monohybrid test cross ratio:
questions.why: In a test cross Aa × aa, half the progeny show the dominant and half the recessive trait: 1 : 1.

questions.q: Enzyme class adding water across bonds:
questions.why: Hydrolases catalyse breaking bonds by adding water (hydrolysis), and form class EC 3.

questions.q: A dsDNA has 35% G. Percentage T:
Lichens are pioneers in:
questions.why: Lichens colonise bare rock first, so they are pioneers in primary succession on rock.

questions.q: Assertion: Sucrose gives a negative Benedict's test. Reason: Both anomeric carbons are involved in the glycosidic bond.
questions.why: Both true: in sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so there is no free reducing group and Benedict's test is negative. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Colour-blind father, normal non-carrier mother: chance a son is colour-blind:
questions.why: A colour-blind father gives his Y to sons, and the colour-blind allele is on X. His sons get X from the non-carrier mother, so the chance is 0.

questions.q: Michaelis constant is 5 mM. v/Vmax at 5 mM:
questions.why: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]). At [S] = Km this equals 1/2 = 0.5.

questions.q: Number of meiotic divisions to produce 100 pollen grains:
questions.why: One meiosis gives 4 pollen grains. For 100 pollen grains, 100/4 = 25 meiotic divisions are needed.

questions.q: Case: Dihybrid test cross gives 45 AB, 5 Ab, 5 aB, 45 ab. Map distance:
questions.why: Recombinants Ab and aB total 5 + 5 = 10 out of 100. RF = 10%, which is 10 cM.

questions.q: A cell with ψ = −0.4 MPa is placed in 0.5 M sucrose (ψ = −1.3 MPa). It will:
questions.why: Water moves toward the more negative water potential. The cell (−0.4) is higher than the sucrose (−1.3), so it loses water and may plasmolyse.

questions.q: In a population, the recessive phenotype is 9%. Frequency of the dominant allele:
questions.why: The recessive phenotype is q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3. The dominant allele frequency p = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.q: Template strand 3′-TACCCGATT-5′ encodes a peptide of how many amino acids?
questions.why: The template 3′-TAC CCG ATT-5′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG GGC UAA-3′, which reads Met–Gly and then stops at UAA. So 2 amino acids.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km from 1 to 3 mM. At [S] = 3 mM, v/Vmax with inhibitor:
questions.why: With the inhibitor, v/Vmax = [S]/(Km,app + [S]) = 3/(3 + 3) = 0.5.

questions.q: Expected DCO 20 in a cross; observed 5. Interference:
questions.why: Coefficient of coincidence = observed/expected = 5/20 = 0.25, so interference = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
